teile.einleitung: St Stephen’s Cathedral is the most famous church in Vienna and a landmark of Austria. The people of Vienna fondly call it the “Steffl”. It stands in the middle of the old town on Stephansplatz.
wichtigste: St Stephen’s Cathedral stands in Vienna on Stephansplatz.
People fondly call it the “Steffl”.
The south tower is about 136 metres high and much taller than the north tower.
The roof is covered with colourful tiles in patterns.
The biggest bell is called the Pummerin.
The catacombs lie beneath the cathedral.

abschnitte.text: **St Stephen’s Cathedral** stands in the middle of **Vienna** on **Stephansplatz**. It is a Catholic church dedicated to Saint Stephen. It was built over many centuries, and large parts date from the **Gothic** period, a style of building with pointed arches and tall windows. In Vienna the cathedral is fondly called the **“Steffl”**.

The **south tower** is about **136 metres** high. For a long time it was one of the tallest buildings in Europe. The **north tower** is much lower, because it was never finished. It was given a small cap instead. If you climb many steps, you get a wide view over the city from the top of the south tower.

Particularly striking is the steep **roof**. It is covered with many **colourful, glazed tiles** that form a **pattern**. On one side you can see a large **double-headed eagle**, an old heraldic animal. On the other side the coats of arms of Vienna and Austria can be seen.

The cathedral’s largest bell is called the **Pummerin**. It is one of the largest bells in Europe. It rings only on special occasions, for example on **New Year’s Eve**. Many people in Austria then hear its ringing on the radio or television. Towards the end of the Second World War the cathedral burned, and afterwards it and the bell were made anew.

Beneath St Stephen’s Cathedral lie the **catacombs**. These are underground passages and rooms with **tombs**. In the past, bishops and members of the Habsburg ruling family were buried here. Today you can visit the catacombs on guided tours.

gewusst: More than 200,000 glazed tiles were used for the roof of St Stephen’s Cathedral.
To reach the watchman’s room in the south tower you have to climb 343 steps.

teile.einleitung: Ulcinj is a town in the far south of Montenegro on the Adriatic. It lies close to the border with Albania. It is known above all for a very long sandy beach.
wichtigste: Ulcinj lies in the far south of Montenegro.
The town lies on the Adriatic close to the border with Albania.
The “Long Beach” at Ulcinj is about 12 kilometres long.
The old town lies on a rock above the sea.
Many inhabitants speak Albanian.

abschnitte.text: South of **Ulcinj** lies the **Long Beach**, in Montenegrin “Velika Plaža”. It is about 12 kilometres long and so one of the longest sandy beaches on the eastern Adriatic. The sand is fine, and the water is shallow at the shore. That is why it is popular with families. At its end lies the river island of **Ada Bojana** on the border with Albania.

The **old town** of Ulcinj lies on a rock high above the sea and is surrounded by walls. The town has a long and eventful history in which various empires ruled it. Many people in Ulcinj belong to the **Albanian** population group. Albanian is therefore often heard in the town. Besides churches there are also many mosques.

gewusst: Near Ulcinj there are large salt pans where many migratory birds rest.

teile.einleitung: The Scandinavian Mountains stretch like a long ridge through Norway and Sweden. They are also called the Scandes. Glaciers have shaped deep fjords and steep rock faces here.
wichtigste: The mountains lie mainly in Norway and Sweden.
They are also called the Scandes.
The highest mountain is Galdhøpiggen in Norway.
The highest mountain in Sweden is Kebnekaise.
Glaciers shaped the fjords on the coast of Norway.
Jostedalsbreen is the largest glacier on the European mainland.

abschnitte.text: The Scandinavian Mountains, also called the **Scandes**, are more than 1,500 kilometres long. They stretch from the south of Norway far into the north. They lie mainly in **Norway and Sweden**, and in the north a little in Finland as well. The mountains are very old, much older than the Alps. Wind, water and ice have worn the mountains down over a long time.

The highest mountain is **Galdhøpiggen** in Norway, at about 2,470 metres. It lies in the Jotunheimen mountains, which means “Home of the Giants”. The highest mountain in Sweden is **Kebnekaise** in the far north. A glacier lies on its southern peak, which is melting because of warming. That is why the summit has become lower in recent years.

In the Ice Age mighty **glaciers** flowed from the mountains to the sea. They carved out deep valleys. Later the sea flooded into these valleys. This is how the **fjords** were formed, long inlets of the sea on the coast of Norway. Large glaciers still exist today. **Jostedalsbreen** is the largest on the European mainland.

In the north of Scandinavia live the **Sami**, a people with their own language and culture. Many Sami keep **reindeer**. Reindeer are deer in which both males and females carry antlers. The herds move back and forth between summer and winter pastures. In summer you can experience the **midnight sun** in the far north: the sun then does not set for weeks.

A well-known sight is **Preikestolen** in southern Norway. It is a flat **rock plateau** that rises about 600 metres vertically above the Lysefjord. The name means “Pulpit Rock”. Every year a great many people hike up to enjoy the view.

gewusst: The Scandinavian Mountains are much older than the Alps.
Kebnekaise has two peaks, and because of the melting ice the northern peak is now the higher one.

teile.einleitung: Plovdiv is the second largest city in Bulgaria and one of the oldest cities in Europe. In 2019 it was a European Capital of Culture together with Matera in Italy.
wichtigste: Plovdiv is the second largest city in Bulgaria.
It is regarded as one of the oldest cities in Europe that are still inhabited today.
In 2019 Plovdiv was a European Capital of Culture, together with Matera.
In the old town stands an ancient Roman theatre.
The city lies on the River Maritsa and is built on hills.

abschnitte.text: People were already living on the site of **Plovdiv** thousands of years ago. The city is regarded as one of the oldest cities in Europe that have been **continuously inhabited** to this day. In antiquity it was conquered by **Philip II** of Macedon, the father of Alexander the Great. It was named **Philippopolis** after him. Later it belonged to the **Roman Empire**.

In the middle of the old town lies a well-preserved **ancient theatre** from Roman times. It was rediscovered only in the 20th century, when a landslide uncovered parts of it. Today concerts and performances take place there again. The remains of a Roman **stadium** also lie under the pedestrian zone.

Plovdiv lies on the River **Maritsa** and is built on several **hills**. In the old town stand colourful houses from the 19th century with overhanging upper floors. In **2019** Plovdiv was a **European Capital of Culture** together with **Matera** in Italy. It was the first time that a Bulgarian city held this title.

gewusst: Like Rome, Plovdiv was founded on seven hills, though not all of them survive today.

teile.einleitung: Slovenia is a small country between the Alps and the Mediterranean. It has high mountains, green forests, a short sea coast and huge stalactite caves. The capital Ljubljana has a dragon as its emblem.
wichtigste: The capital Ljubljana has a dragon as its emblem.
Its neighbours are Austria, Italy, Hungary and Croatia.
The highest mountain is Triglav.
In Lake Bled lies a small island with a church.
The sea coast is only about 47 kilometres long.
The olm lives in the caves.

abschnitte.text: The capital is called **Ljubljana**. Its emblem is a **dragon**, which can also be seen in the city’s coat of arms. Four large dragon figures sit on the famous **Dragon Bridge**. An old legend tells that the Greek hero Jason defeated a dragon here. The River Ljubljanica flows through the old town.

In the north-west lie the **Julian Alps**. **Triglav** stands there, at 2,864 metres the highest mountain in Slovenia. It is even shown on the flag. A popular destination for trips is **Lake Bled**. In the middle of the lake lies a small **island with a church**, which you reach in wooden boats.

Slovenia borders **Austria**, Italy, Hungary and Croatia. The country has been independent since 1991, before which it belonged to Yugoslavia. It has been in the EU since 2004, and since 2007 people have paid with the euro. On the Adriatic Sea Slovenia has only a very short **coast of about 47 kilometres**. Pretty port towns such as Piran lie there.

Slovenia has a great many **caves**. The **Karst** region in the south-west gave this type of rock landscape its name all over the world. You travel into the large stalactite cave of **Postojna** on a **little train**. In the dark caves lives the **olm**. It is a pale, long amphibian without proper eyes and can live to be very old.

gewusst: An olm can live to be over 100 years old.
More than half of Slovenia is covered with forest.

t14muka7.t: Regional policy of the European Union

teile.einleitung: The regional policy of the European Union is meant to ensure that poorer regions can catch up. For this the EU gives money for roads, railways, environmental projects, firms and research. People also speak of cohesion policy, because “cohesion” means holding together.
wichtigste: EU regional policy wants to reduce the differences between rich and poor regions.
A region with a GDP per head below 75 per cent of the EU average counts as less developed.
The European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) was founded in 1975.
The Cohesion Fund pays mainly for transport networks and environmental projects.
Poland received the most funds in the funding periods from 2014.
Switzerland takes part in the Interreg programme.

abschnitte.text: In the EU there are rich and less rich areas. **Regional policy**, also called **cohesion policy**, is meant to reduce these differences. For this the EU distributes money from its common budget. The funds are planned for several years, which are called **funding periods**. The money supports, for example, motorways, railway lines, sewage works, schools or firms.

A **fund** is a pot of money for a particular purpose. The **European Regional Development Fund** (ERDF) was founded in 1975. It supports investment in businesses, research and infrastructure and is now the largest fund of regional policy. The **Cohesion Fund** finances mainly large transport networks and environmental projects. Only countries whose **gross national income** per head is below 90 per cent of the EU average receive money from it.

For funding, the EU divides its territory into regions. What counts is usually the **NUTS 2** level, with regions of about 800,000 to 3 million inhabitants. If the **GDP per head** of a region is below 75 per cent of the EU average, it counts as **less developed** and receives the highest funding rates. GDP is measured here in purchasing power standards so that different prices are taken into account. The largest recipient is **Poland**, which used the money, for example, to modernise motorways and railway lines.

The **additionality principle** is important. It requires that EU money supplements the spending of the states and does not replace it. A country may therefore not simply cut its own investment because money comes from Brussels. In addition, the states have to **co-finance** the projects. Supporters see regional policy as an important contribution to the cohesion of Europe, while critics point to sometimes high costs and a lot of bureaucracy.

Switzerland is not an EU member, but it takes part in the **Interreg** programme. This supports projects across national borders, for example on the Upper Rhine or around Lake Geneva. Switzerland takes part within the framework of its **New Regional Policy**. In addition, with the **enlargement contribution** of about 1.3 billion francs it supported projects in the states that joined the EU from 2004. The people accepted the legal basis for this in 2006.

gewusst: Statistically Switzerland is divided into seven major regions at the NUTS 2 level.
Cohesion policy is among the largest areas of spending in the EU budget.

teile.einleitung: Norway owns one of the largest sovereign wealth funds in the world. The money comes mainly from income from oil and gas. The fund is meant to preserve the wealth for future generations too.
wichtigste: The money comes mainly from income from oil and gas.
Norges Bank Investment Management manages the fund on behalf of the Ministry of Finance.
The Global fund invests only abroad.
Since 2017 the state may spend about 3 per cent of the value of the fund each year.
Since 2004 a Council on Ethics has examined whether companies should be excluded.
The Petroleum Fund was founded by law in 1990.

abschnitte.text: Off the coast of Norway lie large **oil and gas fields**. The state earns a great deal of money by selling them. Norway did not want to simply spend this money straight away. That is why the **Petroleum Fund** was founded by law in **1990**. Today’s **Government Pension Fund** grew out of it. It is meant to secure the wealth for later generations, once the oil has run out.

The large part is called **Statens pensjonsfond utland**, roughly “Government Pension Fund Global”. It is managed by **Norges Bank Investment Management**, a part of the central bank, on behalf of the **Ministry of Finance**. This fund invests **only abroad**. There is also a smaller fund that invests mainly in Norway and the Nordic countries. It is managed by **Folketrygdfondet**.

The fund owns shares in thousands of companies all over the world. In 2025 it held about **1.5 per cent** of the value of all listed companies in the world. In 2026 it was worth more than **20,000 billion kroner**. About **70 per cent** of the money was invested in **shares**. The rest is mainly in bonds and property. The fund also holds shares in many Swiss companies.

So that the money is not used up too quickly, there is a **spending rule**. Since 2017 Norway has been allowed to use roughly as much in the state budget each year as the fund earns on average: about **3 per cent** of the value of the fund. This way the actual capital is kept. It is a little like someone who spends only the interest and keeps the savings.

Norway does not want to use its money to support companies that cause serious harm. Since 2004 a **Council on Ethics** has therefore examined whether companies should be excluded for ethical reasons. Reasons can be, for example, serious environmental damage or the violation of human rights. The Council on Ethics makes recommendations, but the decision is taken by the central bank.

gewusst: In calculation terms, every person in Norway owns a large share of the sovereign wealth fund.
The fund owns shares in thousands of companies in many countries of the world.

teile.einleitung: Vitosha is a mountain range right on the edge of Sofia, the capital of Bulgaria. It is the city’s local mountain and a popular destination for outings. Its highest peak is about 2,290 metres high.
wichtigste: Vitosha is the local mountain of Sofia.
It rises right on the edge of the city.
The range reaches a height of about 2,290 metres.
Vitosha is a nature park.
In summer people hike there, and in winter they go skiing.

abschnitte.titel: A mountain range outside the city
abschnitte.text: **Vitosha** rises right on the southern edge of **Sofia**. You can see the range from many places in the city. The highest peak is called **Cherni Vrah**, which means “Black Peak”. It is about **2,290 metres** high. That makes Vitosha about as high as many mountains in the Swiss Pre-Alps.

Vitosha is a **nature park**. It was founded as early as 1934 and is regarded as the oldest nature park in the Balkans. There are forests, meadows, streams and bogs. Typical are large **stone fields** of round boulders that look like rivers of stone. At the foot of the range stands the old **Boyana Church**, which is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

For the people of Sofia, Vitosha is a popular **destination for outings**. In summer they go **hiking** and picnicking there. In winter you can go **skiing**. Buses and cable cars take you to the range quickly from the city, much as in Zurich you can ride up the Uetliberg.

gewusst: Hardly any European capital has a mountain range over 2,000 metres high so close to its edge as Sofia does.

teile.einleitung: Stromboli is a volcano on a small island north of Sicily. It has been almost constantly active for centuries and throws out glowing lava every few minutes. That is why it is also called the “Lighthouse of the Mediterranean”.
wichtigste: Stromboli belongs to the Aeolian Islands in Italy.
Its summit lies about 920 metres above the sea, and most of the mountain lies under water.
It throws out glowing bits of lava almost continuously at short intervals.
The “Strombolian” type of eruption is named after it.
Lava and rubble slide into the sea over the Sciara del Fuoco.
In December 2002 a landslide there set off a tsunami.

abschnitte.text: Stromboli is one of the most active volcanoes in Europe. For centuries it has hurled glowing **bits of lava** into the air every few minutes. At night you can see the glow from far away. Seafarers used it in the past to find their way. That is why the volcano has the nickname **“Lighthouse of the Mediterranean”**.

A whole type of eruption is named after Stromboli. In a **Strombolian eruption**, large gas bubbles rise in the liquid rock, the **magma**. At the surface they burst and hurl glowing chunks several dozen to hundreds of metres high. The explosions are usually moderately strong and repeat at short intervals. Sometimes, though, there are more violent eruptions.

Stromboli is the north-easternmost of the **Aeolian Islands**, which have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000. Its summit lies about 924 metres above the sea, but most of the volcano is under water. On the north-west slope lies the **Sciara del Fuoco**, the “Slide of Fire”. Ejected material rolls into the sea along this steep channel. The villages therefore lie on the other side of the island.

In December 2002, during an eruption, millions of cubic metres of rock slid from the Sciara del Fuoco into the sea. This created flood waves, a **tsunami**. They damaged houses on the coast of Stromboli and could be felt as far as other islands. Since then experts have monitored the volcano even more closely. Off the north-east coast the rock **Strombolicchio** rises from the sea, the remains of an older volcanic vent, on which a lighthouse now stands.

The director Roberto Rossellini shot the film **“Stromboli”** with Ingrid Bergman right on the island in 1950. A real eruption served as the backdrop, and the island became world famous. Even earlier, the volcano played a part in a novel. In Jules Verne’s **“Journey to the Centre of the Earth”**, the heroes climb down into a volcano in Iceland. At the end they are thrown back to the surface by an eruption of Stromboli.

gewusst: Measured from the sea floor, Stromboli is much higher than it is above the water, because the sea there is more than a thousand metres deep.
On the rock Strombolicchio stands a lighthouse, right next to the natural “lighthouse” Stromboli.

teile.einleitung: Sarajevo is the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The city lies in a valley surrounded by mountains. In 1984 it hosted the Winter Olympic Games, and its history is closely tied to important events in Europe.
wichtigste: Sarajevo is the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The Winter Olympic Games took place in Sarajevo in 1984.
The Swiss athletes Max Julen and Michela Figini won gold there.
In 1914 the Austrian heir to the throne was killed in Sarajevo.
From 1992 to 1996 the city was under siege during the war.
People of different religions live in the city.

abschnitte.text: **Sarajevo** lies on the **Miljacka** river in a valley between mountains. The city was founded in the 15th century by the **Ottomans**. The old bazaar **Baščaršija**, with small shops and workshops, dates from that time. In Sarajevo, mosques, churches and synagogues stand close together. That is why the city is sometimes called the “Jerusalem of Europe”.

In February **1984** the **Winter Olympic Games** took place in Sarajevo. At that time the city belonged to **Yugoslavia**. The ski races were held on the mountains around the city. The mascot was a friendly wolf called **Vučko**. For Switzerland, **Max Julen** won gold in the giant slalom and **Michela Figini** won gold in the downhill.

On 28 June **1914** the Austrian heir to the throne, **Franz Ferdinand**, was shot dead in Sarajevo together with his wife. At that time Bosnia belonged to Austria-Hungary. This **assassination** was the trigger for the **First World War**. The spot by a bridge in the old town still recalls the event today.

When Yugoslavia broke apart, **war** broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina. From **1992 to 1996** Sarajevo was **under siege**, and people suffered from shelling, hunger and cold. Many buildings, including sports venues from 1984, were destroyed. After the war a large part of the city was rebuilt. Today Sarajevo is a lively capital that many visitors come to see.

gewusst: The mascot of the 1984 Winter Games was a wolf called Vučko.
The old bobsleigh track of 1984 on Mount Trebević is now covered with colourful graffiti.

teile.einleitung: Warsaw is the capital and largest city of Poland. It lies on the Vistula and has an eventful history. After the Second World War the destroyed old town was rebuilt.
wichtigste: Warsaw is the largest city in Poland and lies on the Vistula.
The city’s coat of arms shows a mermaid with a sword and shield.
Marie Curie was born in Warsaw in 1867.
The old town was rebuilt after the Second World War.
Since 1980 the old town has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The largest airport is named after Frédéric Chopin.

abschnitte.text: Warsaw lies on both banks of the **Vistula**, the longest river in Poland. Many bridges join the two sides. In 2020 more than **1.8 million people** lived in the city. At the end of the 16th century King **Sigismund III** moved his seat from Kraków to Warsaw. Since about 1600 Warsaw has therefore been the seat of the kings and later the capital.

The coat of arms of Warsaw shows a **mermaid** with a sword and shield. In Polish she is called **Syrenka**. A statue of her stands in the market square of the old town. According to a legend she protects the city.

In the **Second World War** Poland was occupied by Germany. In **1944** the people rose up against the occupation in the **Warsaw Uprising**. It lasted about two months and failed. After that the city was largely destroyed. After the war the **old town** was carefully rebuilt using old pictures and plans. Since **1980** it has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

The scientist **Marie Curie** was born in Warsaw in 1867. She was the first woman to receive a **Nobel Prize**. The composer **Frédéric Chopin** also grew up in Warsaw, and the largest airport is named after him. In the middle of the city stands the **Palace of Culture**, a very tall building from the 1950s. It houses theatres, cinemas and museums.

gewusst: For the rebuilding of the old town, old paintings that showed the city in great detail were used, among other things.
Marie Curie even received two Nobel Prizes, in physics and in chemistry.

teile.einleitung: Slovakia is a country in central Europe without a sea coast. In the north rise the High Tatras, and in the south the Danube flows through the capital Bratislava. Slovakia has been a state of its own since 1993.
wichtigste: The capital is Bratislava on the Danube.
People speak Slovak and pay with the euro.
In the north lie the High Tatra mountains.
The highest mountain is Gerlach Peak.
Slovakia has no sea coast.
The flag is white, blue and red.

abschnitte.text: Slovakia lies in **central Europe** and, like Switzerland, has **no sea coast**. Its neighbours are the Czech Republic, Poland, Ukraine, Hungary and Austria. Until 1992 Slovakia formed **Czechoslovakia** together with the Czech Republic. This was peacefully divided into two states in 1993. Slovakia has belonged to the EU since 2004.

The capital **Bratislava** lies on the **Danube**. A large, four-cornered castle towers above the old town. Bratislava lies right on the border with Austria and Hungary. It is only about 60 kilometres to **Vienna**. Hardly any two other capitals in Europe lie so close together. The second-largest city is **Košice** in the east of the country.

In the north on the border with Poland rise the **High Tatras**. They are the highest part of the Carpathians. Their peaks are rocky and steep, almost like in the Alps. The highest mountain is **Gerlach Peak**, at about 2,650 metres. In the Tatras there are many mountain lakes, and chamois, marmots and bears live there.

The people speak **Slovak**. It is closely related to Czech, so the two peoples understand each other well. Since 2009 people have paid with the **euro**. The flag has three stripes in **white, blue and red**. On the left is a coat of arms with a white double cross on three blue hills.

gewusst: Bratislava and Vienna are the two European capitals that lie closest together.
In Slovakia there are very many castles and castle ruins.

teile.einleitung: The Ruhr area is a large region in the west of Germany in which many cities merge almost seamlessly into one another. In the past it was the most important area for coal and steel in Europe. Today it is a region in transition with museums, universities and a lot of green space.
wichtigste: The Ruhr area lies in the federal state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
It is the largest urban area in Germany.
The largest city is Dortmund, just ahead of Essen.
Hard coal and steel made the region rich from the 19th century.
From 1958 the coal crisis began, and many pits closed.
The last hard coal mine in Germany, Prosper-Haniel in Bottrop, closed in December 2018.
Zollverein colliery in Essen has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2001.

abschnitte.text: The Ruhr area lies in the west of Germany in the federal state of **North Rhine-Westphalia**. It takes its name from the **Ruhr**, which flows into the **Rhine** at Duisburg. The region includes large cities such as Dortmund, Essen, Duisburg, Bochum and Gelsenkirchen. Because the cities lie close together, the area is called a **conurbation**. In Duisburg lies one of the largest inland ports in Europe.

Deep beneath the Ruhr area lie large deposits of **hard coal**. From the 19th century many mines were built, which are called **zechen** in German. The coal was needed for steam engines and for making **steel**. Many people moved from other regions and countries to the Ruhr area to work there. In this way small villages quickly grew into large industrial cities.

From **1958** cheap **imported coal** from abroad and cheap **oil** became more and more important. The expensive Ruhr coal was harder to sell, and the **coal crisis** began. One after another the mines closed, and later many steelworks too. In December **2018** the last hard coal mine in Germany closed with **Prosper-Haniel** in Bottrop. Today most people work in trade, health, education and other services. This change is called the **shift to services**.

Many old plants were not demolished but converted into museums and cultural venues. **Zollverein colliery** in Essen was once regarded as the most beautiful colliery in the world. Together with the neighbouring coking plant it has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2001**. On old spoil heaps there are now works of art and viewpoints. In **2010** Essen was **European Capital of Culture** on behalf of the whole region, and the programme was called **RUHR.2010**.

People often simply call their region the **Revier**, meaning “district”. Football is very popular, and well-known clubs are Borussia Dortmund and Schalke 04. The Ruhr area has several large universities, for example in Bochum, Dortmund and Duisburg-Essen. Rivers that used to be polluted, such as the Emscher, were cleaned at great effort and made more natural again. So the former industrial region is surprisingly green in many places today.

gewusst: Zollverein colliery was once called the “most beautiful colliery in the world” because of its clear design.
With the end of Prosper-Haniel in 2018, a mining tradition about 200 years old came to an end in the Ruhr area.

teile.einleitung: The ABC Islands are Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao. The three islands lie in the Caribbean off the coast of Venezuela. They get their name from the first letters of their names.
wichtigste: ABC stands for Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao.
The islands lie in the Caribbean off the coast of Venezuela.
They used to be Dutch colonies.
Today they belong in different ways to the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

abschnitte.text: The names **Aruba**, **Bonaire** and **Curaçao** begin with A, B and C. That is why people speak of the **ABC Islands**. They lie in the south of the **Caribbean**, not far off the coast of **Venezuela** in South America. The climate is warm and rather dry, and many people visit the islands as a holiday destination.

The three islands were long **Dutch colonies**. Today they all belong to the **Kingdom of the Netherlands**, but in different ways. **Aruba** and **Curaçao** are separate countries within the Kingdom and run many things themselves. **Bonaire**, on the other hand, is a **special municipality** of the Netherlands. Besides Dutch, the language **Papiamento** is often spoken on the islands.

gewusst: On the ABC Islands people speak Papiamento, a language with words from Spanish, Portuguese and Dutch.

teile.einleitung: The Scottish Highlands are the rugged mountain country in the north of Scotland. There are deep lakes, bare hills and only a few villages. The Highlands are well known for Highland cattle, bagpipe music and the Highland Games.
wichtigste: The Highlands lie in Scotland.
Ben Nevis, at about 1,300 metres, is the highest mountain in Great Britain.
The Highland cow with the shaggy coat lives in the Highlands.
The kilt and the bagpipes are typical.
In late summer heather turns the hills purple.
Inverness is regarded as the capital of the Highlands.
The Highland Boundary Fault separates the Highlands from the Lowlands.

abschnitte.text: The **Highlands** are the mountainous north of **Scotland**. They are separated from the flatter south, the **Lowlands**, by a geological fault line, the **Highland Boundary Fault**. Here stands **Ben Nevis**, at about **1,300 metres** the **highest mountain in Great Britain**. By Swiss standards that is not very high, but the weather is often stormy and wet. The region is very thinly populated.

Typical of the Highlands is the **Highland cow** with long horns and a **shaggy coat** that protects it from wind and rain. Red deer and golden eagles also live in the mountains. In **late summer** the **heather** blooms and turns the hills **purple**. In the valleys lie long, deep lakes called **lochs**. The best known is **Loch Ness**.

A well-known item of clothing is the **kilt**, a checked skirt for men. The patterns are called **tartan**, and in the past certain patterns belonged to certain families, the **clans**. The typical musical instrument is the **bagpipes**. In some areas people still speak **Scottish Gaelic**, an old Celtic language. Many place names come from this language.

At the **Highland Games**, athletes compete in traditional contests. The best-known event is the throwing of a long **tree trunk**, the **caber**. The trunk has to flip over in the air. There are also tug of war, stone putting, dancing and bagpipe music. The games are a little reminiscent of Swiss wrestling festivals and stone putting in Switzerland.

The town of **Inverness** is regarded as the **“capital of the Highlands”**. It lies on the River Ness, not far from Loch Ness. From here many visitors explore the Highlands and the Isle of Skye. In the past many small farmers were driven out of the Highlands to make room for large flocks of sheep. That is why many valleys are almost empty of people today.

gewusst: In caber tossing, what counts is not the distance but whether the trunk flips over in a nice straight line.
The shaggy coat protects the Highland cow so well that it can stay outside all winter.

teile.einleitung: The Schengen Area is a region in Europe in which there are no regular checks on people at the borders between the member countries. It is named after the little village of Schengen in Luxembourg. Switzerland belongs to it too, although it is not in the EU.
wichtigste: In the Schengen Area there are no regular checks on people at the internal borders.
The agreement is named after the village of Schengen in Luxembourg.
The first agreement was signed in 1985 on a ship on the Moselle.
Switzerland has applied the agreement since 2008.
In 2025, 29 countries belonged to the Schengen Area.
Ireland is an EU country that does not belong to it.
Bulgaria and Romania joined fully in 2025.

abschnitte.text: In the **Schengen Area** there are no regular **checks on people** at the borders between the member countries, the **internal borders**. You can, for example, travel from Basel to Germany or France without showing your passport. You still have to carry an identity document, though. In return, the **external borders** of the area are checked more closely. In special situations, countries may temporarily bring back border checks.

The first **Schengen Agreement** was signed in **1985**. It happened on a **ship on the Moselle** near the village of **Schengen** in **Luxembourg**. That is where Luxembourg, Germany and France meet. It was signed by **Germany, France** and the three **Benelux states** of Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg. Later more and more countries joined.

Switzerland is not a member of the EU, but it takes part in the Schengen Area. In 2005 the Swiss voters approved the agreement. Switzerland has applied it since **2008**. This also includes cooperation between **police** forces across borders, for example through a shared search database, the **Schengen Information System**. Besides Switzerland, **Norway**, Iceland and Liechtenstein are also part of it, although they do not belong to the EU.

In **2025**, **29 countries** belonged to the Schengen Area. Most of them are members of the EU. Since **2025**, **Bulgaria and Romania** have also been fully included, after checks had at first been dropped only at airports and seaports. **Ireland**, for example, is not part of it, as it has its own shared travel area with the United Kingdom. People coming from outside can often travel to all member countries with a **Schengen visa**.

gewusst: The village of Schengen has only a few hundred inhabitants, but is known all over Europe.
The 1985 treaty was signed on a pleasure boat called the “Princesse Marie-Astrid”.

teile.einleitung: Rovaniemi is a city in the north of Finland and the capital of Finnish Lapland. It lies on the Arctic Circle. It is known to children all over the world as the home of Santa Claus.
wichtigste: Rovaniemi is the capital of Finnish Lapland.
The city lies on the northern Arctic Circle.
On the Arctic Circle stands the well-known Santa Claus Village.
In Rovaniemi the rivers Kemijoki and Ounasjoki meet.
In winter you often see auroras there.

abschnitte.text: The **Arctic Circle** is an imaginary line around the Earth. North of it the Sun does not set on at least one day in summer, and in winter it does not rise on at least one day. **Rovaniemi** lies exactly on this line. So in summer there is the **midnight sun**, and in winter the days are very short. In the city the rivers **Kemijoki** and **Ounasjoki** meet.

A few kilometres north of the city, on the Arctic Circle, lies **Santa Claus Village**. There you can visit Santa Claus and post letters in his post office. Every year letters from children in many countries arrive. Many holidaymakers also travel through the snow by **reindeer** or **husky sleigh**. In winter **auroras** often shine in the sky.

In the **Second World War** Rovaniemi was almost completely destroyed. Afterwards the city was rebuilt. The famous Finnish architect **Alvar Aalto** designed a city plan for it whose main streets are arranged like a **reindeer's antlers**. Today Rovaniemi has a university and the **Arktikum** museum, which informs about nature and people in the far north.

gewusst: The city plan of Rovaniemi is shaped like a reindeer's antlers.
Every year letters from all over the world arrive at Santa Claus's post office.

teile.einleitung: Skerries are small, flat rocky islands off the coasts of Scandinavia and Finland. They were formed when huge glaciers scraped over the rock during the Ice Age. Because the land has been rising ever since, new islands are still emerging from the sea today.
wichtigste: Skerries are small rocky islands smoothed by ice.
A skerry is usually a rounded rock hump that the sea has flooded.
The Stockholm archipelago has about 24,000 islands.
The archipelago off Finland is even larger.
The land has been rising since the Ice Age, so new islands appear.
On the High Coast the land has risen by about 285 metres.

abschnitte.text: In the last **Ice Age**, a thick sheet of ice lay over Scandinavia. The glaciers moved slowly across the land and ground the hard rock smooth. This created round, humped rocks that are called **roches moutonnées**. When the ice melted, sea levels rose. Many of these humps were flooded, and only their backs stick out of the water as **skerries**.

The heavy ice had pressed the land downwards. Since it melted, the ground has slowly been rising again, a bit like a cushion when you get up from it. This is called **land uplift**. On the **High Coast** (Höga Kusten) in Sweden the land has risen by about 285 metres since the Ice Age. Today it is still rising there by about 8 millimetres a year. That is why new rocks and islands keep appearing.

A group of many skerries is called an **archipelago**. The **Stockholm archipelago** consists of about 24,000 islands, rocks and reefs. Even larger is the **Archipelago Sea** off the south-west coast of Finland. There are also skerries on the west coast of Sweden: in the region of **Bohuslän**, reddish granite rocks glow in the sun.

In the Stockholm archipelago lies the small village of **Ytterby**. There used to be a mine there. In the rock at Ytterby, researchers found several new **chemical elements**. Four of them are named after the village: yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium. No other place in the world has given its name to so many elements.

gewusst: On many skerries there is just a single red holiday cottage and a boat jetty.
The High Coast is a UNESCO World Heritage Site because of its land uplift.

teile.einleitung: Romanian is the language spoken in Romania and in Moldova. It belongs to the Romance languages and descends from the Latin of the ancient Romans. This makes it a distant relative of Italian and Romansh.
wichtigste: Romanian belongs to the Romance languages.
It developed from the Latin that was spoken in the Roman province of Dacia.
Romanian is an official language in Romania and in Moldova.
Today Romanian is written with Latin letters.
The definite article is attached to the end of the word.

abschnitte.text: In the year 106 AD the Romans under Emperor **Trajan** conquered the region of **Dacia**, which corresponds roughly to present-day Romania. The people there adopted the **Latin** of the Romans. From this over many centuries Romanian developed. That is why it belongs to the **Romance languages**, like Italian, French, Spanish and Romansh in Graubünden. It is counted in the group of **Balkan Romance** languages.

For a long time Romanian was written with **Cyrillic letters**, as used in Russian today. In the 19th century people switched to the **Latin alphabet**. Some letters have special marks, for example **ă**, **â**, **î**, **ș** and **ț**. The **ș** is pronounced like “sh”, and the **ț** like “ts”. So the Latin word for water, aqua, becomes **apă** in Romanian.

One special feature is the **postposed article**. Instead of putting a word before it as in “the wolf”, the article is attached at the end: **lup** means wolf, and **lupul** means the wolf. Romanian has also taken over many words from neighbouring languages, above all from Slavic languages. The word **da** for “yes”, for example, comes from Slavic. Even so, the basic vocabulary is clearly Latin in character.

gewusst: If you know Italian, you already understand some Romanian sentences a little, because both languages descend from Latin.
Until the 19th century Romanian was mostly written with Cyrillic letters.

teile.einleitung: Christmas markets take place in many European cities during Advent. At the stalls you can buy presents, sweet treats and warm drinks. Some markets are already many hundreds of years old.
wichtigste: Christmas markets mostly take place during Advent.
Typical treats are roasted chestnuts, gingerbread hearts and children’s punch.
The Nuremberg Christkindlesmarkt is opened every year by the Christkind.
Strasbourg calls itself the “Capital of Christmas”.
The Dresden Striezelmarkt has existed since 1434.
In Zurich a large Christmas market takes place in the main station.

abschnitte.text: Christmas markets mostly take place in the weeks before Christmas, that is, in **Advent**. On squares there are small **wooden huts** with lights. There you buy **presents**, candles, decorations for the Christmas tree and treats. In the evening many people meet at the market to have something warm to drink together.

Typical are **roasted chestnuts**, called “Marroni” in Switzerland. They are sold hot in a paper bag in winter. **Gingerbread hearts** with icing writing, hanging from a ribbon, are also popular and often given as presents. Children drink **children’s punch**, a warm fruit juice with spices. **Mulled wine** contains alcohol and is only for adults.

The **Christkindlesmarkt** in **Nuremberg** is world famous. Every year the **Christkind** opens it with a prologue, a ceremonial poem. In **Dresden** the **Striezelmarkt** has existed since **1434**. A “Striezel” is another word for Christmas stollen. **Strasbourg** in Alsace has one of the oldest Christmas markets in France and calls itself the “Capitale de Noël”, the Capital of Christmas.

There are also many Christmas markets in Switzerland. In **Zurich** a large market takes place in the hall of the **main station**, where you are sheltered from rain and snow. In **Montreux** in the canton of Vaud there is the **Montreux Noël** market every year on the shore of **Lake Geneva**. Cities such as Basel and Bern also have large markets.

At many markets you can see a **Christmas pyramid**. It has several storeys with figures. **Candles** burn at the bottom. The warm air rises and turns a **paddle wheel** at the top, which turns the whole pyramid. It comes from the **Ore Mountains** in Germany. At some markets there are huge pyramids several metres high.

gewusst: The Dresden Striezelmarkt is almost 600 years old.
A Christmas pyramid works entirely without electricity, using only the warmth of the candles.

teile.einleitung: Sweden is a large country in the north of Europe. It has many forests, lakes and islands and is the home of Astrid Lindgren. Sweden is a kingdom and has been a member of the European Union since 1995.
wichtigste: The capital of Sweden is Stockholm.
The flag shows a yellow cross on a blue background.
A king is at the head of the state.
People pay with the Swedish krona.
The largest lake is Vänern.
After France and Spain, Sweden is the largest country in the EU by area.

abschnitte.text: Sweden lies on the **Scandinavian Peninsula**. In the west it borders **Norway**, in the north-east Finland. To the east lies the Baltic Sea. The country has huge forests and thousands of lakes. The largest of them is **Vänern**, one of the largest lakes in Europe. After France and Spain, Sweden is the largest country in the EU by area.

Sweden is a **monarchy**: a king is at the head of the state. However, he mainly has ceremonial duties, such as receiving guests of state. Politics is made by parliament, the **Riksdag**, and the government. Since 1995 Sweden, together with Finland, has been a member of the **European Union**. Sweden has not introduced the euro, so people pay with the **Swedish krona**.

The Swedish flag is **blue with a yellow cross**. The cross is shifted a little to one side, as on all the Nordic flags. A popular emblem is the **Dala horse**. It is a small wooden horse, usually painted red, from the province of **Dalarna**. In the past woodcutters carved such horses as toys for children.

The most important summer festival is **Midsummer** in June. The days are very long then, and in the north the sun does not set at all. People decorate a tall **pole** with flowers and leaves and dance around it. Many wear flower wreaths in their hair. There is often herring, new potatoes and strawberries to go with it.

**Astrid Lindgren** was a Swedish children’s author. She wrote **“Pippi Longstocking”**, “Emil of Lönneberga” and “Ronia, the Robber’s Daughter”. Her books have been translated into a great many languages. Almost every child in Switzerland, too, knows Pippi with her red plaits and her horse.

gewusst: In the north of Sweden the midnight sun shines in summer.
The Nobel Prizes are presented in Stockholm every year, except for the Nobel Peace Prize, which is presented in Oslo.

teile.einleitung: At 2,962 metres the Zugspitze is the highest mountain in Germany. It lies in Bavaria on the border with Austria. Railways and cable cars take you right to the summit, where a weather station and a golden summit cross stand.
wichtigste: At 2,962 metres the Zugspitze is the highest mountain in Germany.
The border with Austria runs over the summit.
It is the highest peak of the Wetterstein Mountains.
Small glaciers lie on the Zugspitze.
A rack railway and cable cars lead up the mountain.
At its foot lie Garmisch-Partenkirchen and the Eibsee.

abschnitte.text: The **Zugspitze** is **2,962 metres** high, so almost 3,000 metres. It lies in **Bavaria** and is the highest peak of the **Wetterstein Mountains**. These belong to the **Northern Limestone Alps**. The border with **Austria** runs over the summit. Up there you can walk from one country into the other. In Switzerland there are many higher mountains, but for Germany the Zugspitze is something special.

Small **glaciers** lie on the Zugspitze, for example the Schneeferner. In Germany there are only very few glaciers, and they are getting smaller because of warming. On the summit stands a **weather station**. There **wind**, **temperature** and **snow** have been measured for over 100 years. The golden **summit cross** gleams in the sun and can be seen from far away.

A **rack railway** runs from **Garmisch-Partenkirchen** through a tunnel to just below the summit. A rack railway has a cogwheel that engages in a toothed rail, so it can manage steep stretches. From the **Eibsee** at a height of around 1,000 metres, the **Zugspitze cable car** takes you to the summit in a few minutes. Up top there are viewing terraces with a view of hundreds of peaks.

Below the summit, on the **Zugspitzplatt**, lies a **ski area** that often has snow into spring. In summer mountaineers climb to the summit by various routes. Some routes are long and demanding. You need good equipment and experience, because the weather in the mountains can change quickly.

gewusst: The first known ascent of the Zugspitze was made in 1820.
The gilded summit cross of the Zugspitze is one of the best-known summit crosses in the Alps.

teile.einleitung: The Transfăgărășan is a famous mountain pass road in Romania. With many bends and hairpins it crosses the Făgăraș Mountains in the Southern Carpathians. Many regard it as one of the most impressive mountain roads in Europe.
wichtigste: The Transfăgărășan crosses the Făgăraș Mountains in Romania.
The mountains belong to the Southern Carpathians.
The road was built in the 1970s.
It has a great many bends and hairpins.
Because of snow, it is usually open only in summer.

abschnitte.text: The **Transfăgărășan** crosses the **Făgăraș Mountains**, part of the **Southern Carpathians**. The highest mountains in Romania lie in this range. The road was built in the 1970s, in the time of the dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu. It was also meant to bring troops quickly across the mountains in an emergency. The building work was difficult and dangerous, because a lot of rock had to be blasted.

The road winds up the steep slopes in many **hairpins**. Almost at the top it goes through a tunnel. Near the top of the pass lies the mountain lake of **Bâlea**. From above, the road looks like a ribbon laid over the mountain. Because a lot of snow falls in winter, the road is usually open only in **summer**.

gewusst: The Transfăgărășan is so full of bends that it is popular with motorcyclists and car fans from all over Europe.

teile.einleitung: Moldova is a small country in eastern Europe between Romania and Ukraine. The capital is Chișinău. The country is known for its wine growing and huge underground wine cellars.
wichtigste: The capital of Moldova is Chișinău.
The country lies between Romania and Ukraine and has no access to the sea.
The official language is Romanian.
People pay with the Moldovan leu.
In the east lies the breakaway territory of Transnistria.
In Mileștii Mici lies the largest wine collection in the world.

abschnitte.text: **Moldova** borders **Romania** in the west and **Ukraine** everywhere else. It does not reach the sea. In the west the River **Prut** forms the whole border with Romania. Through the east flows the **Dniester**. The country is hilly and has very fertile, black soils. Since 1991 Moldova has been an independent state, and before that it belonged to the **Soviet Union**.

The capital and largest city is **Chișinău**, in German **Kischinau**. The official language is **Romanian**, which used to be called “Moldovan” there too. In 2023 parliament decided to speak only of the “Romanian language” in all laws. Many people also speak Russian. People pay with the **Moldovan leu**, which was introduced in 1993. It is not the same as the Romanian leu.

**Wine growing** has a very long tradition in Moldova and is an important branch of the economy. In **Mileștii Mici** there are kilometres of underground cellars in an old quarry. About two million bottles are stored there. The Guinness Book of Records lists them as the **largest wine collection in the world**. Visitors even drive through the passages by car.

East of the Dniester lies **Transnistria**. This territory broke away in 1990, and in 1992 there was a short war. Transnistria is recognised by almost no state, and Russian troops are stationed there. In the south lies **Gagauzia**, which has had autonomous status since 1994, so it may manage some things itself. The **Gagauz** speak a language close to Turkish but are Orthodox Christians.

Moldova is among the poorer countries of Europe. Many people work abroad. Since 2022 the country has officially been a **candidate** for accession to the European Union. The direction the country should take is debated internally: some want closer relations with the EU, others with Russia.

gewusst: In the wine cellars of Mileștii Mici the underground passages are named after wine varieties, like streets.
The Gagauz are a Turkic people, but Orthodox Christians.

teile.einleitung: The Vistula is the longest river in Poland. It flows from the south of the country to the north and runs into the Baltic Sea near Gdańsk. Important cities such as Kraków, Warsaw and Toruń lie on its banks.
wichtigste: At around 1,000 kilometres, the Vistula is the longest river in Poland.
In Polish it is called Wisła.
It rises in the Beskids in the south of Poland.
It flows through Kraków, Warsaw and Toruń.
Near Gdańsk it runs into the Baltic Sea.
It is the longest river that flows into the Baltic Sea.

abschnitte.titel: From the Beskids to the sea
abschnitte.text: The Vistula rises on the mountain **Barania Góra** in the **Silesian Beskids**. These belong to the **Carpathians**. From there it flows in a great arc to the north through the whole of Poland. It is about **1,000 kilometres** long, or more exactly around 1,050 kilometres. That makes it the **longest river in Poland** and also the longest river that runs into the **Baltic Sea**. The Daugava and the Neman are shorter.

In the south, **Kraków** lies on the Vistula. For a long time the city was the capital of the **Polish kings**. Above the river stands **Wawel** castle. A legend tells of the **Wawel Dragon**, which lived in a cave by the river beneath the castle. Today a metal dragon figure that breathes fire stands there.

Further north the Vistula flows through the capital **Warsaw**. Many bridges join the two banks there. Even further north lies the city of **Toruń**. There the astronomer **Nicolaus Copernicus** was born in 1473. He realised that the Earth turns around the Sun. The old town of Toruń lies right on the river.

Far in the north the Vistula reaches the sea. Near the port city of **Gdańsk** it runs into the **Baltic Sea**. One arm of the river flows through the city. In the past the Vistula was an important route for bringing **grain** from the interior to the ports. From there it was shipped to other countries.

gewusst: “Wisła” is pronounced roughly “Vissva”.
On the Vistula lie both the old royal city of Kraków and today’s capital, Warsaw.

teile.einleitung: Turku is the oldest city in Finland. It lies in the south-west of the country by the sea and was for a long time the capital. In 1812 the capital was moved to Helsinki.
wichtigste: Turku is the oldest city in Finland.
It was the capital of the country before Helsinki.
In 1812 the capital was moved to Helsinki.
In Swedish the city is called Åbo.
The cathedral and the castle of Turku are well known.

abschnitte.text: **Turku** lies in the south-west of Finland where the River **Aura** flows into the sea. For a long time Finland belonged to Sweden, and Turku was the centre of the country. In Swedish the city is called **Åbo**. In 1809 Finland came under Russian rule. In 1812 the capital was moved to **Helsinki**, which lay closer to Russia.

Landmarks of Turku are the **cathedral**, the most important church in Finland, and the medieval **castle** at the harbour. In 1827 a great fire destroyed part of the city. Today Turku is a university city with many students. Large **ferries** leave the harbour for Sweden. In 2011 Turku was European Capital of Culture.

gewusst: In Turku many people speak Swedish as well as Finnish, which is why the city has two names.

teile.einleitung: Tower Bridge is one of the most famous bridges in the world. It crosses the Thames in London and has two large towers. Its roadway in the middle can open so that tall ships can pass through.
wichtigste: Tower Bridge stands in London and crosses the Thames.
It opened in 1894.
It has two towers joined at the top by two footbridges.
The roadway in the middle consists of two leaves that can be raised.
It is named after the nearby fortress, the Tower of London.
It is often confused with London Bridge.

abschnitte.text: **Tower Bridge** opened in 1894 and is therefore well over 100 years old. It has two large **towers** that recall castle towers. At the top they are joined by two walkways for pedestrians. It gets its name from the **Tower of London**, an old fortress right next to it. Today the bridge is a landmark of London.

Tower Bridge can do something that many other bridges cannot: it can **open**. The roadway in the middle consists of two parts that are raised like **flaps**. This is called a **bascule bridge**. It is necessary because tall ships would otherwise not fit under the bridge. While the leaves are up, cars and pedestrians have to wait.

In the upper walkways there has been a **glass floor** since 2014. If you stand on it, you see cars, buses and ships far below. In the towers there is now an exhibition. There you can also look at the old machines that were once used to move the leaves.

The steel parts of the bridge are now painted **blue and white**. For the Queen’s Silver Jubilee in 1977 the bridge was red, white and blue, like the British flag. Many people wrongly call Tower Bridge **London Bridge**. But London Bridge is a different, much plainer bridge nearby.

gewusst: The old machines of Tower Bridge used to be driven by steam.
Many tourists look for London Bridge and are actually standing in front of Tower Bridge.

teile.einleitung: Norway is the hydropower country of Europe. Around 90 per cent of its electricity comes from hydropower. With its large storage lakes and undersea cables to other countries, Norway plays an important part in Europe’s electricity supply.
wichtigste: Around 90 per cent of Norwegian electricity comes from hydropower.
Norway is the largest hydropower producer in Europe.
The state-owned company Statkraft is the largest producer in the country.
The storage lakes hold about half of Europe’s storage capacity.
Undersea cables connect Norway with Germany, Great Britain and the Netherlands.
Dry years push electricity prices up.

abschnitte.text: Norway has many **mountains**, **lakes** and a lot of **precipitation**. The water flows down from high up to the sea. Hundreds of power plants use this drop. That is how Norway generates around **90 per cent** of its electricity with hydropower, making it the **largest hydropower producer in Europe**. By comparison, in Switzerland it is around 60 per cent. The country’s largest power plant is **Kvilldal**, with an output of about 1,240 megawatts.

In **1905** **Norsk Hydro** was founded. The company used the waterfalls near **Rjukan** and **Notodden** to make **artificial fertiliser**. Hydropower turned Norway into an industrial country early on. The **Vemork** power plant near Rjukan is known in history because heavy water was produced there in the Second World War. Today the state-owned company **Statkraft** is Norway’s largest hydropower producer.

Norway is often called the **battery of Europe**. Its large **storage lakes** hold about half of Europe’s storage capacity. When wind and sun supply a lot of electricity in other countries, Norway can hold the water back. When electricity gets scarce, the water is let through the turbines. In this way Norway helps to balance out swings.

Several **undersea cables** connect Norway with neighbouring countries. **NorNed** opened in 2008 and runs about 580 kilometres to the **Netherlands**. Since 2021 **NordLink** has connected southern Norway over about 620 kilometres with **Schleswig-Holstein** in Germany. **North Sea Link** also went into operation in 2021 and runs about 720 kilometres from Kvilldal to Blyth in **England**. Electricity flows through these cables in both directions.

Hydropower depends on the **weather**. In dry years with little rain and snow, the water levels in the storage lakes fall. Then there is not enough water to generate electricity, and **electricity prices rise** sharply. That is what happened in southern Norway in **2022**, for example. In such times the country imports more electricity from other countries.

gewusst: When they opened, NorNed and North Sea Link were each the longest undersea power cable in the world.
The industrial sites at Rjukan and Notodden are now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: The Black Forest is a large range of low mountains in the south-west of Germany. It is known for dark forests, cuckoo clocks, the Bollenhut hat and Black Forest gateau. In the south it reaches to the Rhine and so close to Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Black Forest lies in the federal state of Baden-Württemberg.
The highest mountain is the Feldberg at 1,493 metres.
Many dark firs and spruces give the forest its name.
The Danube rises in the Black Forest.
In the south the Black Forest ends at the Rhine, with Switzerland beyond.
The cuckoo clock, the Bollenhut and the cherry gateau are world famous.

abschnitte.text: The Black Forest is a **low mountain range**, that is, a range that is not as high as the Alps. It stretches for about 150 kilometres from north to south. Many **firs and spruces** grow on its slopes. These conifers are dark green and stand close together. From a distance the forest therefore looks almost black, which is where the name comes from.

The highest mountain is the **Feldberg**, at 1,493 metres. It is the highest mountain in Germany outside the Alps, and in winter you can ski there. The **Danube** rises in the Black Forest: it is formed from two streams, the Brigach and the Breg. After that it flows right across Europe to the Black Sea. To the west and south the **Rhine** borders the mountains.

The Black Forest lies in the federal state of **Baden-Württemberg**. In the south it ends at the Rhine, and on the other side lies Switzerland. From **Basel** you quickly reach the city of **Freiburg im Breisgau**, which lies right on the edge of the Black Forest. Many people from Switzerland go there on trips for hiking or skiing.

**Cuckoo clocks** have been made in the Black Forest for a long time. In the past farmers carved wooden clocks in winter to earn a little extra. In a cuckoo clock a little door opens on the hour, and a small bird calls “cuckoo”. Today visitors from all over the world buy such clocks as souvenirs.

The **Bollenhut** is part of the traditional costume of some villages in the Black Forest. Large balls of wool sit on the hat. Women who are not yet married wear red balls, and married women wear black ones. Just as famous is the **Black Forest gateau** made of chocolate sponge, cream and cherries. Often a little cherry schnapps is added.

gewusst: The Danube, which begins in the Black Forest, flows through ten countries.
The Bollenhut has become an emblem of the whole Black Forest, although it is part of the traditional costume in only a few villages.

teile.einleitung: The Wadden Sea lies on the coast of the North Sea. Twice a day the water retreats and returns. It is the largest continuous area of tidal flats in the world and an important habitat for many animals.
wichtigste: The Wadden Sea lies on the North Sea in the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark.
At low tide the water retreats, and at high tide it returns.
At low tide you can go mudflat hiking on a guided tour.
Lugworms, seals and millions of migratory birds live there or stop to rest.
Since 2009 the Wadden Sea has been a UNESCO natural World Heritage Site.
Halligen are small islands without a dyke.

abschnitte.text: In the Wadden Sea **low tide** and **high tide** take turns, about every six hours. At low tide the water flows away, and the sea floor becomes visible. This ground of sand and mud is called the **mudflats**. At high tide the water rises again and covers everything. The alternation is called the **tides**. It is caused mainly by the pull of the Moon.

abschnitte.titel: Three countries on the North Sea
abschnitte.text: The Wadden Sea runs along the North Sea coast of the **Netherlands**, **Germany** and **Denmark**. The largest part, around **60 per cent**, belongs to Germany. It is the **largest continuous area of tidal flats** in the world. Since **2009** a large part of it has been a **UNESCO natural World Heritage Site**, and further areas were added in 2011 and 2014. Large parts are also national parks.

At low tide you can walk on the sea floor. This is called **mudflat hiking**. You should only do it with a **guide**. The tide comes back quickly, and deep channels, the **creeks**, fill rapidly with water. Fog can also become dangerous, because you lose your sense of direction.

A great many **worms**, **mussels** and **crabs** live on the mudflats. The **lugworm** lives in a tube in the ground. It eats sand and passes it out again as little coils. At low tide **seals** rest on the sandbanks and also give birth to their pups there. Millions of **migratory birds** take a break in the Wadden Sea because they find plenty of food there.

In the North Frisian Wadden Sea in Germany lie the **Halligen**. These are small islands without a protective dyke. The houses stand on artificial mounds, the **Warften**. In a **storm surge** almost the whole Hallig is under water. This is called “Land unter”, meaning “land under”. Only the Warften with the houses then stick out of the sea.

gewusst: A lugworm eats so much sand that it turns over a large amount of sea floor every year.
During “Land unter”, the houses on the Halligen look as if they were floating in the sea.

teile.einleitung: The reindeer is a deer that lives in the far north. It is perfectly adapted to cold and snow. In Lapland the Sami have kept reindeer for a very long time.
wichtigste: The reindeer is a deer of the far north.
In reindeer both males and females carry antlers.
In winter reindeer scrape through the snow for lichens.
The Sami in Lapland keep reindeer for meat and hides.
In stories reindeer pull Santa Claus's sleigh.
The best-known reindeer from a song is called Rudolph.

abschnitte.text: Reindeer live in cold areas in the north of Europe, Asia and America. In North America wild reindeer are called **caribou**. Unlike most deer, in reindeer both **males and females** carry **antlers**. The antlers are shed every year and then grow again. Reindeer mostly live in large **herds**.

The coat of reindeer is very dense. Its hairs are hollow inside and filled with air, which keeps especially warm. The **hooves** are broad and spread out, so the animals sink less in the snow and in soft bog. With them they can also scrape well for food. When many reindeer walk, you hear a soft **clicking** from their feet.

In summer reindeer eat grasses, herbs and leaves. In winter they scrape through the snow with their hooves for **lichens**. Lichens are special living things made of a fungus and an alga that grow on the ground and on stones. One kind is even called **reindeer lichen**. In search of food, herds often travel long distances.

The **Sami** are a people who live in the north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia. Many Sami families have kept reindeer for centuries. These provide **meat** and warm **hides**. In the past reindeer also pulled sleighs. Today the herders often use snowmobiles to accompany their herds.

In many **Christmas stories** reindeer pull Santa Claus's sleigh through the air. The best known is **Rudolph** with the red nose. In the Christmas song he lights the way through the fog with his nose. Children all over the world know the song.

gewusst: Reindeer are the only deer in which the females regularly carry antlers too.
The hairs in the coat of reindeer are hollow and therefore insulate especially well.

teile.einleitung: The tulip is one of the best-known spring flowers. It grows from a bulb and blooms in many colours. The tulip fields in the Netherlands are especially famous.
wichtigste: Tulips grow from flower bulbs.
The bulbs are put into the ground in autumn.
Tulips bloom in spring, usually in April and May.
Wild tulips originally come from Asia.
At Keukenhof in the Netherlands, millions of flowers bloom every spring.
Around 1637 rare tulip bulbs were extremely expensive in Holland.

abschnitte.text: The **tulip** grows from a **flower bulb**. Food is stored in the bulb, which lets the plant shoot up quickly in spring. The bulbs are put into the ground in autumn. In winter they rest, and in **spring** leaves and a stem with a large flower grow. Tulips usually bloom in April and May and are among the first colourful flowers in the garden.

Wild tulips originally grow in the mountains and steppes of **Asia**. In the **Ottoman Empire**, present-day Turkey, they were grown in gardens early on. In the 16th century tulips came to western Europe. Soon they were bred mainly in the **Netherlands**. Today there are thousands of varieties in almost every colour.

Almost 400 years ago rare tulips were incredibly sought after in Holland. Around 1637 some bulbs cost more than a house. Many people bought bulbs in order to sell them on at a higher price. Suddenly prices fell sharply, and many lost money. This period is called **tulip mania**.

The Netherlands is still the most important country for tulips. In spring huge fields glow there in red, yellow and violet. In the park of **Keukenhof**, millions of flowers bloom every spring, mainly tulips. The park is open for only a few weeks a year. In Switzerland, too, there is a tulip festival, the **Fête de la Tulipe** in Morges on Lake Geneva.

gewusst: A tulip bulb forms small daughter bulbs next to itself, from which new tulips grow.
Tulips often keep on growing in the vase even after they have been cut.

teile.einleitung: The European Union uses “Western Balkans” for several states in south-eastern Europe that are not yet EU members. Most of them used to belong to Yugoslavia. The region has a rich history and went through a difficult time with wars in the 1990s.
wichtigste: The Western Balkans include Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Serbia.
Croatia has been an EU member since 2013 and no longer belongs.
Since 2019 Macedonia has been called North Macedonia, following the Prespa Agreement.
The Dayton Agreement ended the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995.
The Berlin Process has aimed since 2014 to bring the states closer to the EU.
The Swiss Army’s Swisscoy has been deployed in Kosovo since 1999.

abschnitte.text: The term **Western Balkans** comes from the language of the **EU**. It includes **Albania**, **Bosnia and Herzegovina**, **Kosovo**, **Montenegro**, **North Macedonia** and **Serbia**. **Croatia** has been an EU member since **2013** and is therefore no longer counted. Most of these states belonged to **Yugoslavia** until the early 1990s. Many of them would like to join the EU.

When Yugoslavia broke apart, **wars** broke out in the 1990s. In the Bosnian War the famous bridge **Stari Most** in **Mostar** was destroyed in 1993. It dates from the 16th century, was rebuilt exactly as it had been in 2004 and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005. The **Dayton Agreement**, negotiated in Dayton in the USA, ended the war in 1995. It divided the country into two parts, the **Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina** and the **Republika Srpska**.

Macedonia and **Greece** argued for a long time over the name, because Greece has a region of the same name. With the **Prespa Agreement** of 2018 they reached agreement. Since 2019 the country has been called **North Macedonia**. In 2014 Germany launched the **Berlin Process**. It promotes summits and projects on transport, energy and youth exchange.

The Serbian capital **Belgrade** lies where the **Sava** flows into the **Danube**. The **Kalemegdan** fortress overlooks the confluence. The **Bay of Kotor** in Montenegro is surrounded by steep mountains and looks like a fjord. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979. At **Neum**, Bosnia and Herzegovina has only about **20 kilometres** of coast on the Adriatic.

Many people in Switzerland have roots in countries of the Western Balkans. Since **1999** the **Swisscoy** has been deployed in **Kosovo**. This is a voluntary **peace-support mission** of the Swiss Army. It supports the international security force **KFOR**. Switzerland also supports projects for schools, municipalities and business in the region.

gewusst: The narrow strip of coast at Neum separates the Croatian area around Dubrovnik from the rest of Croatia.
The Swisscoy is the Swiss Army’s largest deployment abroad.

teile.einleitung: A sea cliff is a coast with high, steep rock faces. In Europe there are many famous sea cliffs, from the white cliffs of Dover to the red island of Heligoland.
wichtigste: A sea cliff is a coast with high rock faces.
Another word for it is “cliff”.
The waves gnaw at the rocks over time.
The chalk cliffs of Dover are white.
Heligoland has a red sea cliff.
Cabo da Roca is the westernmost point of the European mainland.

abschnitte.text: On a **sea cliff** the land drops steeply into the sea. The **waves** pound again and again against the foot of the rock face. They gnaw a notch into it, called a **wave-cut notch**. If the notch gets too deep, the rock above it breaks off. In this way the sea cliff slowly moves inland.

Some sea cliffs are made of soft, white **chalk**. Very well known are the **white cliffs of Dover** in England on the English Channel. On the German island of **Rügen** in the Baltic Sea there are also famous chalk cliffs, such as the Königsstuhl. In France, **Étretat** lies in Normandy. There the sea has washed beautiful **rock arches** out of the cliffs.

The island of **Heligoland** in the North Sea has a **red sea cliff** of sandstone. Off the coast stands the sea stack called “Lange Anna” (Long Anna). In **Ireland** the **Cliffs of Moher** rise high above the Atlantic. In Portugal lies **Cabo da Roca**. This steep rock is regarded as the **westernmost point** of the European mainland.

Sea cliffs are a safe place for many **seabirds** to breed. On the narrow ledges foxes and other predators can hardly get at them. In the north of Europe the **puffin** breeds there. It has a colourful, triangular beak and is sometimes called the “clown of the sea”. Gulls and gannets also nest on the rocks.

gewusst: A puffin can carry many small fish crosswise in its beak at the same time.
On some sea cliffs several metres of land are lost every year.

teile.einleitung: Pristina is the capital and largest city of Kosovo. On 17 February 2008 Kosovo declared its independence from Serbia there. The city is young and lively, and many of its inhabitants are young people.
wichtigste: Pristina is the capital of Kosovo.
Kosovo declared its independence on 17 February 2008.
On the same day the “Newborn” monument was unveiled in Pristina.
The monument is repainted every year.
In Kosovo people pay with the euro.

abschnitte.text: **Pristina** lies in the east of Kosovo in a hilly area. Most people in the city speak **Albanian**. On **17 February 2008** Kosovo declared its **independence** from Serbia here. Many states have recognised Kosovo as a state of its own, including Switzerland. Other states, such as Serbia, still do not do so today.

In the centre of Pristina stands a special monument: large yellow letters that spell the English word **“Newborn”**. It stands for the new state. The monument was unveiled on the day of the declaration of independence. Since then it has been **repainted** every year, often with a message. Many people sign it or take photos in front of it.

The **National Library** is striking, with its many small domes and a metal lattice around the whole building. Switzerland has close relations with Kosovo. Many people with roots in Kosovo live in Switzerland. In addition, Swiss soldiers have been serving in a peace mission in Kosovo since 1999, in the **Swisscoy**.

gewusst: Kosovo has no currency of its own but uses the euro, although it does not belong to the EU.
The population of Kosovo is among the youngest in Europe.

teile.einleitung: Lake Saimaa is the largest lake in Finland. It lies in the south-east of the country and actually consists of many connected lakes. With its countless islands and bays, it is a popular holiday destination.
wichtigste: Lake Saimaa is the largest lake in Finland.
It lies in the Finnish Lakeland in the south-east of the country.
The lake consists of many connected basins and lakes.
Thousands of islands lie in the lake.
The rare Saimaa ringed seal lives only here.

abschnitte.titel: A lake made of many lakes
abschnitte.text: **Lake Saimaa** is the **largest lake in Finland** and one of the largest lakes in Europe. It is not a simple basin but a network of many lakes, bays and narrow waterways. **Thousands of islands** lie within it. The landscape was formed in the **Ice Age**, when huge glaciers shaped the ground. The lake is part of the **Finnish Lakeland**, an area with a great many lakes.

Towns such as **Lappeenranta** and **Savonlinna** lie on Lake Saimaa. In Savonlinna, the medieval castle of **Olavinlinna** stands on a small island. Opera festivals are held there every summer. Ships can sail from the lake to the Gulf of Finland through the **Saimaa Canal**. The water of the lake flows on via the River Vuoksi towards Lake Ladoga in Russia.

Around Lake Saimaa there are many **forests** and holiday cottages by the water. In summer people go canoeing, swimming or fishing. In winter the lake freezes over, and you can skate on it. Particularly special is the **Saimaa ringed seal**, which lives only in this lake. It is very rare and strictly protected.

gewusst: A species of seal lives in Lake Saimaa that exists nowhere else in the world.

teile.einleitung: Reykjavík is the capital of Iceland. It is the northernmost capital of a sovereign state in the world. The city is heated with hot water from the ground and is the centre of the country.
wichtigste: Reykjavík is the capital of Iceland.
The name means “Smoky Bay”.
It is the northernmost capital of a sovereign state.
Almost all houses are heated with heat from the ground.
About two thirds of the people of Iceland live in the Reykjavík area.
Hallgrímskirkja is the tallest church building in Iceland.

abschnitte.text: The name **Reykjavík** means **Smoky Bay**. The first settlers saw steam rising from hot springs and took it for smoke. According to the Icelandic **Book of Settlements**, **Ingólfur Arnarson** settled in the bay around 874 as the first permanent settler. Reykjavík lies at about **64 degrees north**. No other capital of a sovereign state lies further north.

Iceland lies on many volcanoes, and deep in the ground it is very hot. From boreholes **hot water** is brought up and distributed to the houses through a **district heating network**. This heat from the Earth is called **geothermal energy**. In this way Reykjavík heats almost without oil, gas or coal. The warm water also heats many outdoor **swimming pools**, which are used all year round.

On a hill stands **Hallgrímskirkja**, at about 75 metres the tallest church building in Iceland. It was completed in 1986, and its tower recalls solidified **basalt columns**. At the harbour stands **Harpa**, a concert and conference hall that opened in 2011. Its facade of glass honeycombs was co-designed by the artist **Olafur Eliasson**. In the city centre the Icelandic parliament, the **Althing**, also meets.

In October 1986 the American president **Ronald Reagan** and the Soviet leader **Mikhail Gorbachev** met in the house **Höfði**. They negotiated nuclear **disarmament**, that is, about having fewer nuclear weapons. There was no agreement yet at that time. But the meeting is regarded as a forerunner of later treaties.

Iceland has only just under 400,000 inhabitants. About **two thirds** of them live in the Reykjavík area. Anyone flying to Iceland usually lands at **Keflavík** Airport, about 50 kilometres south-west of the city. The small Reykjavík city airport serves mainly domestic flights.

gewusst: The Icelandic parliament Althing was founded as early as 930 and is regarded as one of the oldest parliaments in the world.
