It is about 3,715 metres high and the highest mountain in Spain.
It is higher than any mountain on the Spanish mainland.
Teide rises within the huge Las Cañadas caldera.
Teide National Park has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007.

abschnitte.text: **Teide** forms the middle of the island of **Tenerife** and can be seen from almost everywhere on the island. At about 3,715 metres it is the highest mountain in Spain. It is even higher than Mulhacén in the Sierra Nevada, the highest mountain on the mainland. In winter there is sometimes snow on its summit while people swim down by the sea. A **cable car** leads up to just below the summit.

Teide is a **volcano**. It grew up inside the **Las Cañadas caldera**. A **caldera** is a huge cauldron that forms when an old volcano collapses in on itself. This caldera has a diameter of about 15 kilometres. Teide is regarded today as dormant, but not extinct. Experts therefore monitor it closely.

Around Teide lies **Teide National Park**. There are lava fields, bizarre rocks and rare plants that grow only here. In 2007 the park was added to the **UNESCO World Heritage** list because of its special volcanic landscape. It is among the most visited national parks in Europe. Because the air up there is often clear, there are also observatories nearby.

gewusst: The original inhabitants of Tenerife, the Guanches, regarded Teide as a sacred mountain.
Measured from the sea floor, Teide is much higher than it is above the sea.

teile.einleitung: Off the coast of Stockholm lie thousands of small rocky islands. They are called skerries, and together they form the Stockholm archipelago. It is a popular destination for trips for people from the city.
wichtigste: The many small rocky islands off Stockholm are called skerries.
Together they form the Stockholm archipelago.
It consists of about 24,000 islands, rocks and reefs.
The skerries were smoothed by ice in the Ice Age.
Many people go by boat to their holiday homes on the islands.

abschnitte.text: Off Stockholm the **Stockholm archipelago** stretches far into the **Baltic Sea**. It consists of about **24,000 islands**, rocks and reefs. Some islands are large and wooded, while others are just bare rocky humps. People live all year round on the larger islands. Many small islands are uninhabited.

The **skerries** were formed in the **Ice Age**. At that time thick glaciers pushed across the land and ground the rocks round and smooth. When the ice melted, the rocks were flooded by the sea. Because the land has been slowly rising since then, new rocks keep appearing out of the water.

Many people from Stockholm have a **summer house** on a skerry. In summer they travel out in their own boat or on a **ferry**. You can swim, sail, go kayaking and pick berries. In winter some bays freeze over, and then you can skate there.

gewusst: In the Stockholm archipelago lies the village of Ytterby, after which four chemical elements are named.

teile.einleitung: The Thracians were an ancient people in the south-east of Europe. They lived mainly in the area of present-day Bulgaria, but also in parts of Greece and Turkey. Their skilfully made gold treasures and burial mounds are famous.
wichtigste: The Thracians lived in the south-east of Europe in ancient times.
Their land was called Thrace and lay mainly in present-day Bulgaria.
They left behind skilfully made gold treasures and burial mounds.
A painted tomb near Kazanlak is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Later Thrace became part of the Roman Empire.

abschnitte.text: The **Thracians** lived more than 2,500 years ago in the area between the Danube, the Black Sea and the Aegean. This area was called **Thrace**. The Thracians consisted of many individual tribes with their own princes. They had contact with the Greeks, who founded cities on the coast. They hardly used a script of their own, so we know a lot from Greek accounts and from finds in the ground.

Particularly well known are the Thracians’ **gold treasures**. Cups, jugs and jewellery made of gold have been found that are very skilfully decorated. Rich princes were buried in **burial mounds**. A painted tomb near **Kazanlak** in Bulgaria is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The area there is also called the “Valley of the Thracian Kings”.

In the first century AD Thrace became a province of the **Roman Empire**. Over time the Thracians mixed with other peoples, and their language disappeared. But traces of their culture can still be found today in museums in Bulgaria and elsewhere.

gewusst: The famous slave Spartacus, who rose up against Rome, came from Thrace.
In Greek legends the singer Orpheus comes from Thrace.

teile.einleitung: Lake Vättern is a large lake in southern Sweden. After Vänern it is the second-largest lake in the country, and it is known for its especially clear water.
wichtigste: Vättern is the second-largest lake in Sweden.
Only Vänern is larger in Sweden.
The lake lies in southern Sweden.
Its water is very clear and clean.
At the southern end lies the town of Jönköping.

abschnitte.text: Vättern lies in the south of **Sweden**. It is long and narrow and much larger than any Swiss lake. After **Vänern** it is the **second-largest lake** in the country. Its water is very **clear**, and you can often see down many metres. Many places on the shore use the lake water as **drinking water**.

At the southern end of the lake lies the town of **Jönköping**. In the south of the lake lies the island of **Visingsö**, where a royal castle once stood. The **Göta Canal** connects Vättern with other lakes and with the sea. In this way ships could once sail right across Sweden.

Because the water is so cold and clean, fish that need such water live in Vättern, for example **char** and **trout**. You also know these fish from mountain lakes in Switzerland. Around the lake there are forests, fields and small villages.

gewusst: Vättern is so clear that in some places you can see down well over ten metres.

teile.einleitung: Romania is a country in the south-east of Europe between the Carpathians and the Black Sea. It is known for castles, mountain forests, the Danube Delta and old villages. Romania has been a member of the European Union since 2007.
wichtigste: The capital of Romania is called Bucharest.
In the east Romania borders the Black Sea.
The Carpathians run in a great arc through the country.
In Romania the Danube flows into the sea in the Danube Delta.
The region of Siebenbürgen is also called Transylvania.
The currency is called the leu.
Romania has been a member of the EU since 2007.

abschnitte.text: Through Romania run the **Carpathians** like a great arc. In their forests many brown bears, wolves and lynxes still live. In the south flows the **Danube**, which forms part of the border with Bulgaria. Shortly before the **Black Sea** it divides into many arms and forms the **Danube Delta**. The delta is a huge wetland with reeds, pelicans and many fish and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In the middle of the country lies **Transylvania**, which is also called **Siebenbürgen** in German. Here there are medieval towns, fortified churches and castles. For a long time German-speaking people also lived here, the **Transylvanian Saxons**. World famous is the spooky figure **Dracula** from an English novel by Bram Stoker from 1897. The name recalls a real prince of the 15th century, Vlad III, who bore the nickname Drăculea.

The capital **Bucharest** is the largest city in the country. There stands the **Palace of the Parliament**, one of the largest buildings in the world. It was built under the dictator **Nicolae Ceaușescu**, who ruled the country strictly. In December 1989 his rule was ended in a revolution. After that Romania became a democracy and joined NATO in 2004 and, together with Bulgaria, the **European Union** in **2007**.

In Romania people speak **Romanian**, a Romance language related to Italian and French. The currency is called the **leu**, which means “lion”, and the plural is lei. In the countryside many people still live from farming. Typical dishes are maize porridge, called **mămăligă**, and stuffed cabbage leaves. Many Romanians also live and work in other countries of Europe, some of them in Switzerland.

Romania is known for strong gymnastics. At the Olympic Games in Montreal in **1976** the young gymnast **Nadia Comăneci** was the first person ever to receive a score of **10**. The scoreboards had not been built for this and therefore showed “1.00”. Nadia Comăneci won several gold medals in Montreal and became world famous.

gewusst: At Nadia Comăneci's perfect score the scoreboard showed only “1.00”, because nobody had expected a 10.
The name of the currency leu means “lion” in English.

teile.einleitung: The Rhine is one of the most important rivers in Europe. It rises in the Swiss Alps and flows through several countries to the North Sea. On its way it passes many cities and carries large ships.
wichtigste: The Rhine is about 1230 kilometres long.
It forms from the Anterior Rhine and the Posterior Rhine at Reichenau in Graubünden.
The Rhine flows through Lake Constance.
At Schaffhausen it plunges over the Rhine Falls.
Basel has Rhine ports for large ships.
Near Rotterdam the Rhine flows into the North Sea.

abschnitte.text: The Rhine has two headstreams. The **Anterior Rhine** flows from the small **Lake Toma** at a height of just over 2300 metres near the Oberalp Pass. This lake is often regarded as the **source of the Rhine**. The Anterior Rhine flows through the **Ruinaulta**, a gorge that it cut into the debris of the **Flims rockslide**. This rockslide happened about 9500 years ago. At **Reichenau** it joins the **Posterior Rhine** to form the Rhine.

abschnitte.titel: Lake Constance and the Rhine Falls
abschnitte.text: As the **Alpine Rhine** the river flows past Liechtenstein and Austria into **Lake Constance**. At **Stein am Rhein** it leaves the lake again. At **Neuhausen am Rheinfall** near Schaffhausen it plunges over rocks into the depths. The **Rhine Falls** are among the largest waterfalls in Europe. After that the river is called the **High Rhine** and mostly forms the border between Switzerland and Germany.

In **Basel** lie the **Swiss Rhine Ports**. From here ships can travel on the Rhine to the sea. In this way Switzerland, despite having no sea coast, is connected with the world's oceans. The ships carry, for example, crude oil, grain and containers. The Rhine is one of the most important rivers for **shipping** in Europe.

After Basel the Rhine flows north and for a stretch forms the border between France and Germany. Later it flows through a narrow valley with many **castles** and vineyards. There also stands the well-known rock **Loreley**. In **Cologne** the **Cologne Cathedral**, one of the largest churches in the world, stands right on the bank.

In the **Netherlands** the Rhine divides into several arms. Near **Rotterdam** it reaches the North Sea. Rotterdam has the largest port in Europe. In all the Rhine is about **1230 kilometres** long and flows through or along six countries.

gewusst: A drop of water from Lake Toma takes many days to reach the North Sea.
The Ruinaulta is also called the “Swiss Grand Canyon”.

teile.einleitung: Alexander von Humboldt was a German naturalist and one of the most famous travellers in history. From 1799 to 1804 he explored South America and Central America. His reports made the nature of the Americas known in Europe.
wichtigste: Alexander von Humboldt was born in Berlin in 1769.
From 1799 to 1804 he travelled mainly through South America.
His companion was the French botanist Aimé Bonpland.
In 1802 he climbed to a record height on Chimborazo.
He confirmed that the Casiquiare connects the Orinoco and the Amazon.
His great late work is called “Kosmos”.

abschnitte.text: Alexander von Humboldt was born in **1769** in **Berlin**, which then belonged to **Prussia**. His brother **Wilhelm von Humboldt** was a linguist and educational reformer. He helped to found the University of Berlin. Today it is called the **Humboldt University** and bears the name of the two brothers.

From **1799 to 1804** Humboldt travelled through the Americas. He visited present-day **Venezuela**, **Colombia**, **Ecuador**, **Peru** and **Mexico**, and at the end the USA. He was accompanied by the French botanist **Aimé Bonpland**. Together they collected thousands of plants and measured temperatures, heights and much more.

In **1800** Humboldt and Bonpland travelled up the **Orinoco**. He examined the river **Casiquiare** and confirmed that it connects the river system of the Orinoco with that of the **Amazon**. Such a natural connection between two great river systems is very rare.

In **1802** Humboldt climbed the volcano **Chimborazo** in Ecuador. He reached around **5,600 metres**, but not the summit. For a long time this was the greatest height that a human being had demonstrably reached. Humboldt observed how the plant life changes with height.

From **1845** Humboldt’s late work in several volumes, **“Kosmos”**, appeared. In it he wanted to describe the knowledge about the whole world, and it was a great success. The **Humboldt Current** is named after him. This **cold ocean current** flows north off the west coast of Chile and Peru and brings nutrient-rich water.

gewusst: Many things are named after Humboldt, including an ocean current, the Humboldt penguin and places on several continents.
Humboldt understood nature as a connected whole in which everything is linked.

teile.einleitung: The Pyrenees are a mountain range in the south-west of Europe. They form the natural border between France and Spain and stretch from the Atlantic to the Mediterranean. In the middle of the mountains lies the small country of Andorra.
wichtigste: The Pyrenees separate France and Spain.
They stretch about 430 kilometres from the Atlantic to the Mediterranean.
The highest mountain is Aneto at about 3404 metres.
The Pyrenees are lower than the Alps.
The small country of Andorra lies in the middle of the Pyrenees.
At the western end live the Basques with their own language.

abschnitte.text: The **Pyrenees** are about **430 kilometres** long. They stretch from the **Atlantic** in the west to the **Mediterranean** in the east. To the north lies **France**, to the south **Spain**. The range bounds the north of the **Iberian Peninsula**, on which Spain and Portugal lie. In the middle of the mountains lies the small country of **Andorra**, which is entirely mountainous.

The highest mountain is **Aneto** in Spain at about **3404 metres**. This makes the Pyrenees **lower than the Alps**, where many peaks are over 4000 metres high. In the east stands **Canigou**, in Catalan Canigó, about 2780 metres high. It is regarded as the holy mountain of the **Catalans**. Every year on St John's Day a fire is lit on its summit.

At the western end of the Pyrenees, on the Atlantic, live the **Basques**. Their territory lies partly in Spain and partly in France. Their language, **Basque**, is related to no other known language. In the east live the **Catalans**, who speak Catalan. In Andorra too Catalan is the official language.

In the Pyrenees there were almost no **brown bears** left. So bears from **Slovenia** were brought there and resettled. This is controversial with some people, especially shepherds. Typical of the mountains is also the Pyrenean chamois. In French it is called the **isard**. It is somewhat smaller than the chamois in the Alps.

On the French side lies the **Cirque de Gavarnie**, a huge basin with steep rock walls and high waterfalls. Glaciers shaped it in the ice age. Together with the area around **Monte Perdido** on the Spanish side it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Many people hike on long-distance trails through the whole range.

gewusst: On the summit of the Pic du Midi de Bigorre stands an observatory, that is, a place for observing the sky.
Basque is one of the oldest languages in Europe and is related to no other language.

teile.einleitung: Hungary is a country in the middle of Europe with no sea coast. It is known for its capital Budapest on the Danube, Lake Balaton, paprika and goulash. The people speak Hungarian, a very special language.
wichtigste: The capital of Hungary is Budapest.
Balaton is the largest lake in central Europe.
In Hungary people pay with the forint, not with the euro.
Paprika and goulash are typical of Hungarian cooking.
Hungarian is hardly related to German or the Slavic languages.
In the west Hungary borders Austria.
The highest mountain, Kékes, is only 1,014 metres high.

abschnitte.text: The **capital Budapest** lies on both banks of the **Danube**. About one in five people in the country live there. In the past Buda and Pest were two separate cities, which were joined by bridges. On the bank stands the large **Parliament building** with its dome. In Budapest there are also many **thermal baths**, fed by warm springs.

Hungary is a rather **flat country** without high mountains. A large part belongs to the **Pannonian Plain**, which in Hungary is also called the **Puszta**. The highest mountain, **Kékes**, is only 1,014 metres high. Hungary has no sea coast. In the west it borders **Austria**, and its other neighbours include Slovakia, Romania and Croatia.

**Lake Balaton** is the largest lake in central Europe. In summer many families go there to swim, because the water is shallow and warms up quickly. Very close by lies **Lake Hévíz**. It is fed by a warm spring and is one of the largest thermal lakes in the world. Even in winter the water is warm enough for swimming.

Hungary is famous for its red **paprika powder**. It goes into many dishes and gives them colour and flavour. The best-known dish is **goulash**, a stew with meat and paprika. In the past **cattle herders** cooked it in a cauldron over an open fire. Goulash is often on the menu in Switzerland too.

In Hungary people speak **Hungarian**. The language belongs to a family of its own and is distantly related to Finnish, but hardly to German. People pay with the **forint**, although Hungary belongs to the European Union. The Hungarian **Ernő Rubik** invented the **Rubik’s Cube** in 1974. You have to twist it so that each side shows only one colour.

gewusst: The Rubik’s Cube from Hungary is among the best-selling toys in the world.
In Lake Hévíz you can swim in warm water even in the middle of winter.

teile.einleitung: The Pelješac Bridge is a large bridge in the south of Croatia. Since 2022 it has linked the mainland with the Pelješac peninsula, so that you can drive to Dubrovnik within Croatia.
wichtigste: The Pelješac Bridge opened in 2022.
It leads from the Croatian mainland to the Pelješac peninsula.
Before that, on the way to Dubrovnik you had to drive a short stretch through Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The bridge is about 2.4 kilometres long.
The European Union helped to finance its construction.

abschnitte.text: The coast of Croatia is very long. But near the town of **Neum**, **Bosnia and Herzegovina** reaches the sea with a short stretch. The area around **Dubrovnik** was therefore cut off by land from the rest of Croatia. Anyone driving to Dubrovnik by car had to cross a **border** twice.

The **Pelješac Bridge** leads from the mainland over the sea to the **Pelješac peninsula**. From there you continue towards Dubrovnik. This means you can drive within Croatia without crossing a border. The bridge is about **2.4 kilometres** long and opened in the summer of **2022**. The **European Union** paid a large part of the costs.

**Pelješac** is a long, hilly peninsula. It is known for **wine** and for **oysters** from the bay near **Ston**. At Ston there are also long old **town walls** from the Middle Ages. In the past they protected the salt pans, which were very valuable to Dubrovnik.

gewusst: The walls of Ston are among the longest defensive walls in Europe.
The bridge was built by a Chinese construction company.

teile.einleitung: Slættaratindur is the highest mountain in the Faroe Islands. The Faroe Islands are a group of islands in the North Atlantic between Scotland, Norway and Iceland. The mountain stands on the island of Eysturoy and is about 880 metres high.
wichtigste: Slættaratindur is the highest mountain in the Faroe Islands.
It is about 880 metres high.
It stands on the island of Eysturoy.
The Faroe Islands lie in the North Atlantic.
In clear weather you can see all the Faroe Islands from the summit.

abschnitte.text: The **Faroe Islands** consist of 18 islands in the North Atlantic. They lie between Scotland, Norway and Iceland. The Faroe Islands belong to the Kingdom of **Denmark**, but manage many things themselves. The islands are steep, green and almost without trees. Strong winds often blow, and the weather changes quickly.

**Slættaratindur** stands in the north of the island of **Eysturoy**. It is about **880 metres** high. That does not sound like much, but the mountain rises almost straight out of the sea. The name means roughly “flat peak”, because the top of the mountain is quite flat. A hiking trail leads up it.

abschnitte.titel: A view over all the islands
abschnitte.text: In **clear weather** you can see all the Faroe Islands from the summit. Often, though, clouds and fog hang around the mountain. That is why good equipment is important. Around the longest day in June, many people in the Faroe Islands climb to the summit to experience the bright night there.

gewusst: There are far more sheep than people in the Faroe Islands.

teile.einleitung: Poland is a large country in central Europe with the capital Warsaw. It lies on the Baltic Sea and has a long and eventful history. Famous people such as Nicolaus Copernicus and Frédéric Chopin came from Poland.
wichtigste: The capital of Poland is Warsaw.
Poland lies in the north on the Baltic Sea.
The Vistula is the longest river in Poland.
Poland borders seven countries, Germany in the west.
In Poland people pay with the złoty.
The flag is white at the top and red at the bottom.

abschnitte.text: Poland lies in **central Europe**. In the north it has a long coast on the **Baltic Sea** with many sandy beaches. In the middle the country is mostly flat, and in the south there are mountains such as the **Tatras**. The longest river is the **Vistula**. It flows from the mountains in the south through Kraków and Warsaw to the Baltic Sea. In the west the rivers **Oder** and **Neisse** form a large part of the border with Germany.

Poland borders **seven** countries: Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Ukraine, Belarus, Lithuania and Russia with the Kaliningrad region. Since 2004 Poland has been a member of the **European Union**. It has not introduced the euro, however. People pay with the **złoty**, which means “golden”. The flag has two stripes: **white** at the top and **red** at the bottom.

For many centuries **Kraków** was the capital of Poland. There, on a hill, stands the **Wawel** castle, where the Polish kings lived. Around 1600 the royal court moved to **Warsaw**, which is today the capital and largest city. In the Second World War Warsaw was almost entirely destroyed. The old town was then carefully rebuilt.

**Nicolaus Copernicus** lived about 500 years ago. He recognised that the Earth goes round the Sun and not the other way round. This changed the picture of the universe. The composer **Frédéric Chopin** was born in Poland in 1810 and wrote mainly music for the piano. The scientist **Marie Curie** also came from Warsaw.

After the Second World War Poland was led by a communist government. In 1980 workers at the shipyard in **Gdańsk** went on strike and founded the free trade union **Solidarność**, which means “Solidarity”. A trade union is an association of employees. The movement helped Poland become a democracy peacefully in 1989.

gewusst: In Rapperswil on Lake Zurich there has been a Polish museum in the castle since 1870.
Marie Curie was the first person to receive two Nobel Prizes.

teile.einleitung: The flow regime describes how much water a river typically carries over the course of a year. Some rivers are full in summer, others in winter or spring. That depends on whether glaciers, snow or rain mainly feed the river.
wichtigste: The flow regime is the typical annual pattern of discharge.
In the glacial regime the maximum falls in July and August.
The nival regime is shaped by snowmelt.
Rivers in the Central Plateau and Jura often have a pluvial, that is rain-shaped, regime.
The Pardé coefficient compares each month with the annual mean.
Lakes even out the discharge of a river.

abschnitte.text: The **discharge** is the amount of water that flows past one point of a river in a second. The **flow regime** shows in which months a river carries a lot or little water on long-term average. It depends on **precipitation**, **snow**, **glaciers** and **evaporation**. To compare rivers of different sizes, the **Pardé coefficient** is used: the mean monthly discharge divided by the mean annual discharge. Values above 1 mean months with plenty of water.

In the **glacial regime** glaciers melt mainly in high summer. That is why these rivers carry the most water in **July and August** and very little in winter. In the **nival regime** the **snowmelt** determines the discharge, “nival” coming from the Latin “nix” for snow. The maximum is usually in late spring or early summer. In the **pluvial regime**, from “pluvia” for rain, the discharge depends mainly on rain. That is the case for many rivers in the **Central Plateau** and in the **Jura**: they often carry more water in winter and spring and little in late summer.

Large lakes act like a **reservoir**. In a flood they take in a lot of water and release it with a delay. In this way they dampen discharge peaks and raise the discharge in dry periods. You can see this with the **Rhine**: below **Lake Constance** its discharge is more even than above it.

In Switzerland the **Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN)** runs the national network of discharge measuring stations. Its hydrology division measures water level and discharge at numerous stations. The course of the discharge over time is shown in a **hydrograph**. In a flood you can see the rise, the peak and the fall in it.

Because of climate warming, the glaciers in the Alps are melting. At first they therefore supply **more water**. But when they keep getting smaller, this source is missing. In the long run, rivers with a glacial regime will therefore carry **less water** in high summer. That affects hydropower and agriculture, for example.

gewusst: In high summer a glacier stream can carry much more water in the afternoon than in the morning, because the ice melts during the day.
Lake Constance evens out the discharge of the Rhine so much that flood peaks below the lake are much flatter.

teile.einleitung: The Stari Most, in English the “Old Bridge”, is a famous stone bridge in the city of Mostar in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was built in the 16th century, destroyed in the war in 1993 and reopened in 2004. Today it is a symbol of reconciliation.
wichtigste: The Stari Most stands in Mostar in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
It spans the River Neretva.
It was built in the 16th century, when the Ottomans ruled.
In 1993 it was destroyed in the war.
In 2004 it was reopened.
Since 2005 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: The **Stari Most** spans the green **Neretva** river in a single, high **arch**. It was completed in 1566, when the area belonged to the **Ottoman Empire**. For its time, the wide arch was a great achievement of the builders’ art. The city of **Mostar** gets its name from the bridge: the bridge keepers were called “mostari”.

In the **Bosnian War** the bridge was destroyed in **1993**. This made many people all over the world sad. After the war many countries helped with the **rebuilding**. Stones were taken from the Neretva for this, and old techniques and plans were used. In **2004** the bridge was ceremonially reopened.

For a long time young men have jumped from the bridge into the Neretva. The bridge is more than 20 metres high, and the water is very cold. Only experienced **jumpers** dare to do it. Every summer there is a well-known **competition**. Since **2005** the bridge, together with the old town of Mostar, has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: For the rebuilding, stones that came from the old bridge were recovered from the river.

teile.einleitung: Accra is the capital of Ghana in West Africa. The city lies on the Atlantic coast on the Gulf of Guinea. It is the political and economic centre of the country.
wichtigste: Accra is the capital and largest city of Ghana.
The city lies on the Gulf of Guinea, that is, on the Atlantic.
In 1877 Accra became the capital of the British Gold Coast.
The Black Star Gate commemorates the independence of Ghana.
The second-largest city in Ghana is Kumasi.

abschnitte.text: Accra lies right on the **Gulf of Guinea**, a part of the **Atlantic**. The city is the **largest city in Ghana** and an important port and trading place. The second-largest city in the country is **Kumasi**, which lies inland. Accra is home to the government, many companies and universities.

abschnitte.titel: From the Gold Coast to Ghana
abschnitte.text: The area of present-day Ghana was a British colony and was called the **Gold Coast**. In **1877** the British moved their seat of administration from **Cape Coast** to Accra. Since then Accra has been the political centre. In **1957** Ghana became independent, as one of the first countries south of the Sahara. Accra remained the capital.

On **Independence Square** in Accra stands the **Black Star Gate**, a large gateway with a black star. It commemorates the **independence** of Ghana. The **black star** is a symbol of the country and also stands in the middle of the flag. The national football team is also called the “Black Stars”.

gewusst: In 1957 Ghana was one of the first African countries south of the Sahara to become independent.
The Ghana national football team is called the “Black Stars”, like the star on the flag.

teile.einleitung: Prague is the capital of the Czech Republic and lies on the Vltava. With its many towers, bridges and old houses it is among the most beautiful cities in Europe. The old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: Prague is the capital of the Czech Republic and lies on the Vltava.
Charles Bridge is over 600 years old.
Prague Castle is among the largest castle complexes in the world.
Prague is called the “City of a Hundred Spires”.
Charles University, founded in 1348, is regarded as the oldest university in central Europe.
The writer Franz Kafka was born in Prague in 1883.

abschnitte.text: Through Prague flows the **Vltava**, which later flows into the Elbe. Many bridges cross the river. The most famous is the stone **Charles Bridge**. It is over 600 years old and named after Emperor **Charles IV**. Many stone figures stand on it. Today only pedestrians may cross it.

On a hill above the Vltava stands **Prague Castle**. It is one of the largest castle complexes in the world. In the middle stands **St Vitus Cathedral** with its tall towers. In the past kings and emperors lived here, and today the **president** of the Czech Republic works here.

abschnitte.titel: The old town and the Astronomical Clock
abschnitte.text: On the Old Town Hall hangs the **Astronomical Clock**, which is about 600 years old. It shows not only the time but also the positions of the Sun and Moon. On the hour **figures of the apostles** pass small windows, and many people watch. Many houses in the old town have **red tiled roofs**. Because of the many church and gate towers, Prague is also called the **City of a Hundred Spires**.

In 1348 Emperor Charles IV founded **Charles University**. It is regarded as the oldest university in central Europe. Vienna followed in 1365, and the University of **Basel**, the oldest in Switzerland, only in 1460. In Prague **Franz Kafka** was born in 1883. He wrote his books in German, because at that time many people in Prague spoke German and Czech.

abschnitte.titel: Wenceslas Square and the Dancing House
abschnitte.text: In the New Town lies the long **Wenceslas Square**, named after Saint Wenceslas. At its upper end stands the **National Museum**. Here in 1989 many people gathered during the peaceful protests against the communist government. Quite modern is the **Dancing House**, which was finished in 1996. Its two curving towers recall a dancing couple.

gewusst: The Astronomical Clock of Prague is one of the oldest clocks of its kind that still work.
Prague Castle is so large that it is like a small town with churches, palaces and lanes.

teile.einleitung: The Sami are a people in the far north of Europe. They live in Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia and have their own languages, songs and symbols. These include their own flag and their own national day.
wichtigste: The Sami live in the north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia.
They call their homeland Sápmi.
The Sami national day is on 6 February.
The Sami flag has the colours red, blue, green and yellow.
For many Sami, reindeer herding is culturally important.

abschnitte.text: The **Sami** are the **indigenous people** of northern Scandinavia and of the Russian Kola Peninsula. They call their homeland **Sápmi**. In the past they were also called “Lapps”, but today that word is considered insulting. Traditionally many Sami kept **reindeer**, while others lived from fishing. The **joik**, a special Sami style of singing, is also well known.

The Sami **national day** is on **6 February**. On that day in **1917**, Sami from different countries met for the first time at a large assembly in Trondheim in Norway. They wanted to stand up for their rights together. Today many places hoist the Sami flag on that day, and many people wear their traditional clothing.

The **Sami flag** was adopted in **1986**. It has the colours **red, blue, green and yellow**, which also appear in traditional Sami clothing. In the middle is a **circle**, half red and half blue. The red part stands for the **sun**, the blue part for the **moon**. The flag is for all Sami, no matter which country they live in.

gewusst: The circle on the Sami flag stands for the sun and the moon.
6 February commemorates the first large Sami assembly in 1917.

teile.einleitung: The Czech Republic is a country in the middle of Europe. The capital is Prague, and people pay with the Czech koruna. Like Switzerland, the Czech Republic has no sea coast.
wichtigste: The capital of the Czech Republic is Prague.
People pay with the Czech koruna.
The Czech Republic is a landlocked country without a sea coast, like Switzerland.
Until the end of 1992 it formed Czechoslovakia together with Slovakia.
The two large parts of the country are called Bohemia in the west and Moravia in the east.
The highest mountain is Sněžka in the Giant Mountains.

abschnitte.text: The **Czech Republic** lies in central Europe and is a **landlocked country**, that is, a country without a sea coast, just like Switzerland. In the south it borders Austria. Its other neighbours are Germany, Poland and Slovakia. The highest mountain is **Sněžka** in the Giant Mountains on the border with Poland, about 1,600 metres high. The **Elbe**, which flows through Germany into the North Sea, also rises in the Giant Mountains.

The Czech Republic consists mainly of two large parts. In the west lies **Bohemia** with the capital **Prague**. The Vltava flows through Prague, and the famous Charles Bridge crosses it. In the east lies **Moravia** with the city of **Brno**. Brno is the capital of Moravia and the second-largest city in the country.

For a long time the Czech Republic and Slovakia belonged together as **Czechoslovakia**. On 1 January 1993 they separated peacefully into two countries. Since 2004 the Czech Republic has been a member of the **European Union**. It has not introduced the euro, though. People still pay with the **Czech koruna**, just as in Switzerland they pay with the franc.

One of the best-known cartoon characters in the world comes from the Czech Republic: **the Little Mole**. He was invented by the Czech illustrator **Zdeněk Miler**. The mole has many adventures with his animal friends. The films get by almost without words. That is why children all over the world understand them.

gewusst: In Czech the Little Mole is called “Krtek”.
The Elbe, which flows into the North Sea at Hamburg, begins in the mountains of the Czech Republic.

teile.einleitung: Algeria lies in North Africa on the Mediterranean and is the largest country in Africa by area. Most of the country belongs to the Sahara. The capital is Algiers.
wichtigste: Since 2011 Algeria has been the largest country in Africa.
The capital is called Algiers.
In 1962 Algeria became independent from France.
Over four fifths of the area belong to the Sahara.
The most important exports are oil and natural gas.
The currency is the Algerian dinar.

abschnitte.text: Algeria covers around **2.38 million square kilometres**. Since **South Sudan** split from Sudan in 2011, it has been the **largest country in Africa**. The capital **Algiers** lies on the Mediterranean coast and is also the largest city. The country is named after the city. People pay with the **Algerian dinar**.

Algeria was French for over **130 years**. Many Algerians wanted a state of their own. After a long **war of independence** the country became independent in **1962**. To this day many people in Algeria speak French as well as Arabic and Berber languages.

More than **80 per cent** of Algeria is desert, and it belongs to the **Sahara**. Most people therefore live on the narrow coastal strip on the Mediterranean. In the middle of the Sahara rises the **Ahaggar**, also called the **Hoggar**. It is a mountain range of volcanic origin. Its highest peak, **Tahat**, is 2,908 metres high.

In the **Tassili n’Ajjer** there are thousands of ancient **rock paintings**. They show animals such as **giraffes** and **cattle**. These animals need water and plants. So the pictures prove that the Sahara used to be **green**. The area is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Algeria lives mainly from selling **oil** and **natural gas**. These raw materials lie beneath the desert. The gas is also delivered to Europe through **pipelines** under the Mediterranean, for example to Italy and Spain.

gewusst: The rock paintings in the Tassili n’Ajjer show giraffes in the middle of today’s Sahara.
Tunisia and Libya also pay with a dinar.

teile.einleitung: The Storting is the parliament of Norway. It meets in the capital Oslo and makes the laws of the country. The name means roughly “great assembly”.
wichtigste: The Storting is the parliament of Norway and sits in Oslo.
The name means roughly “great assembly”.
The members are elected by the people every four years.
Norway is a monarchy with a king, but the laws are passed by the Storting.
The Norwegian constitution dates from 1814.

abschnitte.text: The **Storting** is the representative body of Norway. Here the members discuss and pass the laws and the state budget, that is, what the state’s money is spent on. It meets in a building from the 19th century in the middle of **Oslo**. The word is made up of “stor” for great and “ting” for assembly. Even the Vikings met in assemblies, which they called a “Thing”.

The members of the Storting are elected by the people every **four years**. Unlike in many countries, the parliament cannot be dissolved early. Norway is a **constitutional monarchy**: there is a king, but he mainly has ceremonial duties. The government needs the support of the Storting. In Switzerland, the **Federal Assembly** with the National Council and the Council of States corresponds to the Storting, but it has two chambers.

The Norwegian **constitution** was adopted in Eidsvoll in 1814. It is among the oldest constitutions still in force in the world. 17 May, Constitution Day, is still the national day of Norway. On this day many children march in parades through the streets with flags.

gewusst: The Storting elects the members of the committee that awards the Nobel Peace Prize every year.
A parliament with the word part “ting” also exists in Denmark: there it is called the Folketing.

teile.einleitung: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean and belongs to Italy. It lies off the toe of the boot and is roughly triangular in shape. It is known for the volcano Etna, lemons, oranges and ancient Greek temples.
wichtigste: Sicily lies off the toe of Italy’s boot.
The island is roughly triangular in shape.
The capital is Palermo.
Etna is a large, active volcano.
The Strait of Messina separates Sicily from the mainland.
Well-preserved Greek temples stand near Agrigento.

abschnitte.text: If you look at the map, Italy looks like a **boot**. Off the toe of the boot lies **Sicily**, the largest island in the Mediterranean. It is roughly the shape of a **triangle**. The capital is **Palermo** on the north coast. Between Sicily and the mainland lies a narrow strait, the **Strait of Messina**.

In the east of the island stands **Etna**. It is the highest active volcano in Europe and more than 3,000 metres high. Again and again it spews out ash and lava. The people nearby still like living there, because the volcanic soil is very **fertile**. Since 2013 Etna has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

There is **no bridge** between Sicily and the mainland. Anyone travelling to Sicily by train experiences something special: the carriages are pushed onto a **ferry**. The ship takes them across the Strait of Messina. On the other side the train carries on along the rails.

In Sicily the sun often shines, and it is warm. That is why especially many **lemons and oranges** grow there. Almonds, olives and pistachios also thrive. Sweet specialities such as cannoli, filled pastry rolls, and granita made of frozen fruit juice are well known.

More than 2,500 years ago **Greeks** founded cities in Sicily. Near **Agrigento**, in the so-called **Valley of the Temples**, stand some of the best-preserved Greek temples in the world. Later Romans, Arabs, Normans and other peoples ruled the island. All of them left traces, in buildings, food and words.

gewusst: The flag of Sicily shows a head with three legs, which stand for the three corners of the island.
Etna is so big that snow often lies on its summit while lemons grow down by the sea.

teile.einleitung: Alaska is the largest state of the USA. It lies in the far north-west of North America and is separated from the rest of the USA by Canada. Alaska is known for mountains, glaciers, bears and northern lights.
wichtigste: Alaska is the largest state of the USA.
The USA bought Alaska from Russia in 1867.
Since 1959 Alaska has been the 49th state.
The capital is Juneau, and the largest city is Anchorage.
Denali is the highest mountain in North America.
On land Alaska borders only Canada.

abschnitte.titel: Huge and far in the north
abschnitte.text: By a wide margin Alaska is the **largest state** of the USA, more than twice as big as Texas. In the east it borders **Canada**, which is its only land border. To **Russia** there is only a sea passage, the **Bering Strait**. The capital is **Juneau**. The largest city, however, is **Anchorage**, where around 40 per cent of the population lives.

Alaska used to belong to **Russia**. In **1867** the USA bought the territory for **7.2 million dollars**. After that Alaska was a **territory** of the USA for a long time. In January **1959** it became the **49th state**.

In Alaska stands **Denali**, the highest mountain in **North America**. It is over 6,100 metres high. That makes it much higher than the **Dufourspitze**, the highest peak in Switzerland. Around the mountain lies a large national park.

In summer the **salmon** swim up the rivers. Then **brown bears** wait at the water and catch the fish with their paws and mouths. Alaska has a lot of untouched nature. Besides bears, moose, wolves and bald eagles also live there.

In the night sky in Alaska you can often see the **northern lights**. They glow green or pink and can be seen above all in regions close to the North Pole. Every year the famous **Iditarod** takes place. In this **dog sled race** people travel with their dogs well over 1,000 kilometres through snow and ice.

gewusst: Alaska is more than twice as big as Texas, the second-largest state.
At the narrowest point of the Bering Strait, Alaska and Russia are only about 80 kilometres apart.

teile.einleitung: Spain is one of the sunniest countries in Europe. That is why solar energy plays a big role there. In southern Spain there are large solar power plants, research centres and huge photovoltaic parks.
wichtigste: Southern Spain has high solar radiation and many hours of sunshine.
PS10 near Seville was Europe’s first commercial solar tower power plant in 2007.
Gemasolar uses a solar tower with salt storage.
The Andasol power plants work with parabolic troughs and heat storage.
Large photovoltaic parks stand in Extremadura.
In 2018 Spain abolished the so-called sun tax.

abschnitte.titel: Plenty of sun in the south
abschnitte.text: Southern Spain has **high solar radiation** and very many **hours of sunshine** a year. The sky is often cloudless, and there are wide areas with few buildings. This is ideal for **solar energy**, that is, electricity and heat from sunlight. There are two main technologies: **photovoltaics** turns light directly into electricity. With **concentrated solar power**, mirrors focus the light to produce heat.

Near **Seville** the **PS10** power plant went into operation in 2007. It was Europe’s first commercial **solar tower power plant**. Many mirrors direct the sunlight to the top of a tower. It becomes very hot there, and the heat is used to make steam for a turbine. The **Gemasolar** power plant also stores the heat in **molten salt**. This means it can supply electricity at night as well.

In the province of **Granada** stand the **Andasol power plants**. They use long, curved mirrors called **parabolic troughs**. These heat a liquid in a pipe. A **heat store** holds the energy for several hours. In the province of Almería lies the **Plataforma Solar de Almería**, a large research centre for concentrated solar power.

In the region of **Extremadura** stand huge **photovoltaic parks** such as Núñez de Balboa and Francisco Pizarro. For private individuals there was long a controversial charge on solar power they used themselves, the so-called **sun tax**. Spain abolished it in **2018**. After that many more people put solar panels on their roofs.

On **28 April 2025** there was a **large-scale blackout** on the Iberian Peninsula. Spain and Portugal were without electricity for hours. Afterwards there was much discussion about how a power grid with a great deal of solar power can stay **stable**. Experts investigated the causes. Storage and power plants that balance out fluctuations in the grid are important, for example.

gewusst: A solar tower power plant with salt storage like Gemasolar can supply electricity at night too.
The mirrors of a solar tower follow the sun across the sky.

teile.einleitung: The Po Valley is the largest plain in Italy. It lies in the north of the country between the Alps and the Apennines and is crossed by the Po, the longest river in Italy.
wichtigste: The Po Valley lies in northern Italy between the Alps and the Apennines.
The Po is about 650 kilometres long and the longest river in Italy.
The Po rises on Monte Viso and flows into the Adriatic south of Venice.
The River Ticino comes from Switzerland and joins the Po near Pavia.
A lot of rice is grown in the Po Valley, for example for risotto.
In autumn and winter dense fog often lies over the plain.

abschnitte.text: The Po Valley is surrounded by mountains on three sides: in the north and west by the **Alps** and in the south by the **Apennines**. To the east it opens onto the Adriatic. In the past there was a basin here that was covered by the sea. Over millions of years rivers brought sand, gravel and mud from the mountains and filled up the basin. Such deposited material is called **sediment**. That is why the ground is so flat and fertile today.

The **Po** rises on **Monte Viso** in the Cottian Alps, near the border with France. It flows east and passes **Turin**, the capital of Piedmont. Many tributaries from the Alps flow into it, including the **Ticino**. This rises in the canton of Ticino, flows through Lake Maggiore and reaches the Po near Pavia. At its mouth in the **Adriatic** the Po forms a large **delta**, that is, an area where the river divides into many arms.

The Po Valley is the most important farming region in Italy. Around **Vercelli**, **Novara** and **Pavia** lie huge rice fields, which are flooded with water. Italy is the largest rice producer in Europe, and **risotto** is often cooked from this rice. Maize, wheat, fruit and vegetables also grow here. Well-known cheeses such as Parmesan are made from the milk of the cows.

Very many people live in the Po Valley and on its edge. Large cities are **Milan**, Turin, Bologna and Verona. There are many factories, companies and important transport routes here. For Switzerland the region is an important neighbour: over the Gotthard and the Simplon, rail and road lead straight into the Po Valley.

In autumn and winter the damp, windless plain is often foggy, much like the Swiss Plateau. Cold air often lies at the ground with warmer air above it. This weather situation is called an **inversion**. Exhaust gases from traffic, industry and heating then cannot escape. That is why the Po Valley often has one of the worst air qualities in Europe in winter.

gewusst: The Po Valley was once a sea basin that was filled up with debris by rivers.
Water from the Ticino in the canton of Ticino flows by way of the Po as far as the Adriatic.

teile.einleitung: Salzburg is a city in Austria close to the German border. It is famous as the birthplace of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and for its magnificent old town. Every summer people from all over the world come to the Salzburg Festival.
wichtigste: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756.
His birthplace stands in the Getreidegasse.
The Hohensalzburg Fortress towers above the city.
The Salzach flows through Salzburg.
The city is named after salt.
The Salzburg Festival has existed since 1920.
The old town has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996.

abschnitte.text: Salzburg lies on the **Salzach** and is the capital of the Austrian federal state of Salzburg. The name comes from **salt**, which was mined in the surrounding area and transported on the river. Salt used to be very valuable and was also called “white gold”. For a long time **archbishops** ruled the city and had magnificent churches and palaces built. Salzburg has only belonged to Austria since the 19th century.

High above the city stands the **Hohensalzburg Fortress**. It was begun in the 11th century and is one of the largest castles in Europe still standing. A funicular railway runs up to it. Below lie the **cathedral**, narrow lanes and many squares with fountains. Because the old town is so well preserved, it has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since **1996**.

**Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart** was born in Salzburg in 1756. His **birthplace** stands in the **Getreidegasse** and is now a museum. As a child Mozart already played the piano and the violin and travelled across Europe with his father. Later he wrote famous operas such as “The Magic Flute”. The **Mozartkugeln** are also well known, round sweets made of marzipan, nougat and chocolate.

Since **1920** the **Salzburg Festival** has taken place every summer, with opera, concerts and theatre. Its founders included the director Max Reinhardt and the poet Hugo von Hofmannsthal. Every year the play “Jedermann” is performed on the Cathedral Square. The musical film **“The Sound of Music”** from 1965, about the singing Trapp family, is also world famous. Many scenes were filmed in and around Salzburg.

**Salzburger Nockerl** are a sweet speciality. They are made of fluffy whisked egg white with sugar and a little flour and are baked in the oven. Three golden-brown mounds dusted with icing sugar are meant to recall the **three mountains** around the city, which look snow-covered. You have to eat them at once, or they collapse.

gewusst: Many people in Salzburg hardly know “The Sound of Music”, while the film is very famous in the USA.
Salzburger Nockerl represent three snow-covered mountains around the city.

teile.einleitung: San Marino is a very small country completely surrounded by Italy. It lies on Mount Titano and is regarded as the oldest surviving republic in the world. From the top you can see as far as the Adriatic Sea.
wichtigste: San Marino is a very small country in the middle of Italy.
The capital is also called San Marino and lies on Mount Titano.
San Marino is regarded as the oldest republic in the world.
Three towers stand on the mountain.
The country has two heads of state at the same time.
People pay with the euro.
The seaside town of Rimini lies nearby.

abschnitte.text: **San Marino** is one of the smallest states in the world. At about 61 square kilometres, it is roughly a quarter the size of the canton of Zug. About **34,000 people** live in the country. San Marino is completely surrounded by **Italy**, so it is an **enclave**. Not far away lies the well-known seaside town of **Rimini** on the Adriatic.

The capital is also called **San Marino** and lies high up on **Mount Titano**. On the mountain ridge stand **three towers**, which can also be seen in the coat of arms and on the flag. From there you have a wide view across the country as far as the sea. The old town and Mount Titano are a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. The country is divided into nine municipalities, which are called **Castelli**.

According to legend, the stonemason **Marinus** founded San Marino in the year 301. He is said to have settled on the mountain so that he could live in peace as a Christian. Later he was venerated as **Saint Marinus**, and the country was named after him. Because San Marino has been a republic for such a long time, it is regarded as the **oldest republic in the world**. It remained independent over the centuries, although many empires arose and disappeared all around it.

San Marino has **two heads of state** at the same time, the **Captains Regent** (Capitani Reggenti). They are elected by parliament and govern for only **six months**. Then two other people take over the office. This is meant to make sure nobody gets too much power. It is a little reminiscent of Switzerland, where the President of the Confederation changes every year.

In San Marino people pay with the **euro**, although the country does not belong to the European Union. San Marino mints its own euro coins, which are popular with collectors. Its own postage stamps are also well known. Many visitors come as day trippers from the seaside resorts on the coast. Tourism is an important source of income.

gewusst: San Marino’s two heads of state change every six months.
The three towers on Mount Titano are also shown on the flag of San Marino.

teile.einleitung: Scotland is a part of the United Kingdom in the north of the island of Great Britain. It has a long history of its own, its own parliament and wild landscapes. The capital is Edinburgh, and the largest city is Glasgow.
wichtigste: Glasgow is the largest city in Scotland, and Edinburgh is the capital.
The thistle is a national symbol of Scotland.
Ben Nevis, at 1,345 metres, is the highest mountain in the United Kingdom.
In 1707 Scotland and England joined together with the Act of Union.
In 2014 about 55% voted to remain in the United Kingdom.
Skara Brae on Orkney is a Stone Age village.
A “firth” is a broad sea inlet or river mouth.

abschnitte.text: Scotland lies in the **north of Great Britain** and belongs to the **United Kingdom**. The capital is **Edinburgh**, with its castle on a rock. The **largest city**, however, is **Glasgow**. Scotland also includes almost 800 islands, such as the **Hebrides** and the **Orkney** and **Shetland Islands**. The flag shows a white diagonal cross on a blue background, the **St Andrew’s Cross**.

The highest mountain in the United Kingdom is **Ben Nevis**, at **1,345 metres**. A great fault line, the **Great Glen Fault**, runs right across the Highlands. **Loch Ness** lies in this long valley. A **firth** is a broad **sea inlet** or **river mouth**, for example the Firth of Forth near Edinburgh. A national symbol is the prickly **thistle**.

On the Orkney Islands lies **Skara Brae**, a very well preserved **Stone Age village**. The houses even have beds and shelves made of stone. The **Orkney** and **Shetland Islands** long belonged to the realm of **Denmark-Norway**. In 1468/69 they were pledged to Scotland as part of a princess’s dowry, and so came to Scotland. That is why many traces of the Vikings can still be found there today.

Scotland was a kingdom of its own for a long time. With the **Act of Union**, Scotland and England joined together in **1707** to form the Kingdom of **Great Britain**. In the 18th and 19th centuries many small farmers were driven out of the Highlands to make room for sheep. These evictions are called the **Highland Clearances**. Many of those affected emigrated to America or Australia.

Since 1999 Scotland has once again had its **own parliament** in Edinburgh, which decides on schools, health and much more. In **2014** there was a **referendum** on independence. About **55%** voted to **remain** in the United Kingdom. The question of whether Scotland should become independent is still debated today. Referendums are much rarer there than in Switzerland, though.

gewusst: The Stone Age village of Skara Brae is older than the pyramids of Giza.
The Orkney and Shetland Islands came to Scotland as a pledge for a dowry.

teile.einleitung: Sveti Stefan is a small place on the coast of Montenegro, near the town of Budva. The old fishing village lies on a rocky island joined to the mainland. Since the 1950s the whole village has been a hotel.
wichtigste: Sveti Stefan lies on the Adriatic coast of Montenegro near Budva.
The place stands on a small rocky island.
A narrow strip of land joins the island to the mainland.
It used to be a fishing village with houses of stone.
Since the 1950s the whole village has been used as a hotel.

abschnitte.text: Sveti Stefan means “Saint Stephen”. The village lies on a small **rocky island** in the Adriatic. A narrow strip of sand joins it to the mainland, so that you can walk across. The houses are made of stone and have red tiled roofs. From a distance the place looks like a small castle in the sea. It is one of the best-known photo subjects in **Montenegro**.

Fishing families lived here for a long time. Later many inhabitants moved away. In the 1950s the whole village was converted into a **hotel**. The old stone houses became guest rooms. The hotel became famous, and many well-known guests stayed there. Today most people can only admire the island from the outside, but the beaches next to it are easy to reach.

gewusst: At Sveti Stefan a whole village is at the same time a single hotel.

teile.einleitung: The Alps are the highest mountain range lying entirely in Europe. They stretch in a great arc from France to Slovenia and also shape a large part of Switzerland. Their highest peak is Mont Blanc.
wichtigste: The Alps extend in an arc over around 1,200 kilometres.
Eight states have a share of the Alps.
The highest mountain in the Alps is Mont Blanc at around 4,800 metres.
The highest peak in Switzerland is the Dufourspitze at 4,634 metres.
The Alps were formed because the African plate pushes against the Eurasian plate.
Large rivers such as the Rhine, Rhône, Po and Inn rise in the Alps.
About two thirds of Switzerland belong to the Alps.

abschnitte.text: The Alps reach from the area around Nice on the Mediterranean to Vienna. Eight states have a share: **France**, Monaco, Italy, **Switzerland**, Liechtenstein, Germany, Austria and Slovenia. Austria and Italy have the largest shares. In Switzerland the Alps cover the south and the middle of the country.

The Alps are a young **fold mountain range**. They formed because the African plate is slowly pushing against the Eurasian plate. Layers of rock were pushed together, folded and forced upwards, over many millions of years. In the **Ice Ages** huge glaciers shaped the valleys and scoured out lakes.

**Mont Blanc**, on the border between France and Italy, is the highest mountain in the Alps at around 4,800 metres. The **Dufourspitze** in the Monte Rosa massif is the highest peak in Switzerland at 4,634 metres. In all, there are over 80 four-thousanders in the Alps. Famous mountains also include the Matterhorn, the Eiger and the Jungfrau.

In the Alps live **ibexes**, chamois, marmots and bearded vultures. The higher you climb, the smaller the plants become: forests are followed by alpine pastures, then rocks and glaciers. Well-known alpine flowers are the edelweiss and the gentian. Many animals have adapted to cold and snow, the ptarmigan, for example, turns white in winter.

About 14 million people live in the Alps. In the past the **passes** such as the Gotthard or the Great St Bernard were important but dangerous trade routes. Today long tunnels run through the mountains, for example the **Gotthard Base Tunnel**, which opened in 2016 and at 57 kilometres is the longest railway tunnel in the world. Many people live from tourism, in winter from skiing and in summer from hiking.

Large rivers such as the **Rhine**, the Rhône, the Po and the Inn rise in the Alps. Their water flows into the North Sea, the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. That is why the Alps, and Switzerland in particular, are also called the **water tower of Europe**. The largest glacier in the Alps is the Great Aletsch Glacier in the Valais.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mountain range that forms when layers of rock are pushed together and folded.
A mountain that is at least 4,000 metres high.
A lower point in a mountain range over which a path or road runs.
A great stream of ice that moves slowly down the valley.

gewusst: The Alps still grow about one millimetre higher every year, while at the same time erosion wears them down.
On the Matterhorn, rock was found that originally belonged to the African plate.
The glaciers of the Alps have shrunk greatly since 1850.

teile.einleitung: The Black Sea is a large inland sea between Europe and Asia. Six states border its coasts. Even the water of the River Inn from the Engadine reaches it via the Danube.
wichtigste: The Black Sea lies between Europe and Asia.
Six states border it.
The water of the Inn from the Engadine flows via the Danube into the Black Sea.
The Crimean Peninsula juts into the sea from the north.
In the north the Sea of Azov is connected to it.
Dolphins live in the Black Sea.
The deep water contains almost no oxygen.

abschnitte.text: The **Black Sea** lies between **Europe and Asia**. Through the **Bosphorus** at Istanbul it is connected to the Sea of Marmara and onwards to the Mediterranean. In the north it is joined by a strait to the small **Sea of Azov**. The **Crimean Peninsula** juts into the sea from the north. **Six states** border the Black Sea: Turkey, Bulgaria, Romania, Ukraine, Russia and Georgia.

Large rivers such as the **Danube**, the Dnieper and the Dniester flow into the Black Sea. The **Inn** rises in the **Engadine** and flows into the Danube at Passau. In this way water from the Grisons ends up in the Black Sea. Because so much fresh water flows in, the sea is less salty than the oceans. Before it reaches the sea in Romania, the Danube forms a large delta.

On the coast lie many port and holiday towns. In **Bulgaria**, **Varna** is a well-known port city with beaches. In **Ukraine** lies the port city of **Odessa** with its famous staircase. In **Sochi** in Russia, the **Winter Olympic Games** took place in **2014**, even though the city lies by the sea. The ski races took place in the mountains behind the city.

**Dolphins** live in the Black Sea, for example the bottlenose dolphin, as well as small porpoises. They live only in the upper layers of water, though. The **deep water** contains **almost no oxygen**, because the water hardly mixes. Instead there is the poisonous gas **hydrogen sulphide** there, and almost only bacteria can survive. Because wood hardly decays there, very old, well-preserved **shipwrecks** are found on the sea floor.

gewusst: A drop of water from the Engadine can travel via the Inn and the Danube all the way to the Black Sea.
On the floor of the Black Sea lie shipwrecks that are more than 2,000 years old and astonishingly well preserved.

teile.einleitung: A windmill uses the force of the wind to drive a machine. In the past windmills ground grain or pumped out water. Today modern wind turbines generate electricity.
wichtigste: In the past windmills often ground grain into flour.
In the Netherlands many mills pumped out water.
At Kinderdijk stand 19 old windmills, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997.
A typical Dutch windmill has four sails.
Modern wind turbines generate electricity, also in the Swiss Jura.

abschnitte.text: In many windmills heavy **millstones** turned. The wind drove the **sails**, and the stone moved by way of gear wheels. This is how **grain was ground into flour**, from which bread was baked. Most old windmills have **four big sails**. So that the sails always face the wind, with many mills the whole mill or its cap can be turned.

abschnitte.titel: Pumping out water in the Netherlands
abschnitte.text: A large part of the **Netherlands** lies very low, partly below sea level. That is why many mills pumped **water** from the low land into the **canals**. In this way fields and villages stayed dry. At **Kinderdijk** stand **19 old windmills** along canals. They have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since **1997**.

With the **post mill** the whole mill house is turned on a post to face the wind. With the **tower mill** the tower stays put, and only the **cap** with the sails is turned. Windmills also sawed wood or pressed oil from seeds. In Switzerland, watermills on streams and rivers were much more common than windmills.

Modern **wind turbines** usually have three long rotor blades. They turn a **generator** that produces **electricity**. Wind power is a **renewable energy**, because the wind never stops completely. There are also a few wind turbines in Switzerland, for example in the **Jura**. Large wind farms stand mainly on coasts and at sea.

gewusst: In the famous story of Don Quixote, the hero takes windmills for giants and fights them.
The mills of Kinderdijk are among the best-known photo subjects in the Netherlands.

teile.einleitung: Europe is one of the most popular travel destinations in the world. Millions of people visit its cities, beaches, mountains and museums every year. Tourism brings in a lot of money, but it can also cause problems.
wichtigste: France is the most visited travel destination in the world.
In 2024 Spain counted about 94 million foreign visitors.
The Louvre in Paris is the most visited art museum in the world.
Overtourism means that too many tourists put a strain on a place.
Since 2024 Venice has charged day visitors an entrance fee on certain days.
In Switzerland the Jungfraujoch and Zermatt are popular destinations.

abschnitte.text: **France** is the most visited travel destination in the world. About 100 million foreign visitors come every year, for example to Paris, to the Côte d’Azur or to the Alps. In Paris stands the **Louvre**, the most visited art museum in the world, with almost 9 million visitors a year. The Mona Lisa hangs there too. **Spain** is also very popular and set a record in 2024 with about 94 million foreign visitors.

Many people take beach holidays on the **Mediterranean**. In Spain, for example, the **Costa Brava** between Barcelona and the French border is popular. The name means “wild coast”, because it has many rocky bays. In Barcelona stands the **Sagrada Família**, a huge church by the architect **Antoni Gaudí**. He worked on it for more than 40 years, and it is still not finished.

Switzerland also lives to a large extent from **tourism**. On the **Jungfraujoch**, at 3,454 metres above sea level, lies the highest railway station in Europe. It is marketed as the “Top of Europe” and attracts visitors from all over the world. At the foot of the Matterhorn lies **Zermatt**. No ordinary cars with combustion engines drive there. Visitors arrive by train and get around the village in electric vehicles.

Tourism creates jobs in hotels, restaurants and mountain railways. But in some places so many people come that residents, nature and sights suffer. This is called **overtourism**. Examples are Venice, Barcelona or Hallstatt in Austria. **Venice** has therefore charged day visitors an entrance fee on certain days since 2024. The aim is to steer the flow of visitors and protect the old town.

gewusst: The Sagrada Família has been under construction for more than 140 years.
Zermatt has been closed to ordinary cars for decades.

teile.einleitung: Hydropower means using the force of flowing or falling water to generate electricity. In Europe it is especially important in countries with mountains and a lot of rain. Switzerland, too, gets a large part of its electricity from hydropower.
wichtigste: Hydropower plants turn the force of water into electricity.
Norway generates about 90 per cent of its electricity with hydropower.
In Switzerland about 60 per cent of electricity comes from hydropower.
The Grande Dixence in the Valais is the tallest gravity dam in the world.
At the Iron Gates two large power plants dam the Danube.
Hydropower is a renewable energy.

abschnitte.text: When water flows or falls, it contains **energy**. In a hydropower plant the water flows through a **turbine** and turns it. The turbine drives a **generator**, which produces **electricity**. The more water and the greater the drop, the more electricity is produced. Because the rain keeps supplying the water, hydropower counts as a **renewable energy**.

**Run-of-river power plants** stand on rivers and use the water that happens to be flowing past. **Storage power plants** collect water in a **reservoir** behind a dam. This means electricity can be produced when it is needed. **Pumped-storage power plants** pump water uphill when there is surplus electricity and let it flow back down later. In Switzerland there are all three types.

Switzerland has many mountains, glaciers and rivers. That is why about **60 per cent** of Swiss electricity comes from hydropower. In the canton of **Valais** stands the **Grande Dixence** dam. It is 285 metres high and the **tallest gravity dam in the world**. It dams the **Lac des Dix** in the Val d’Hérémence. A gravity dam holds back the water simply through its enormous weight.

The leader in Europe is **Norway**. Thanks to many mountains, lakes and rainfall, the country generates about **90 per cent** of its electricity with hydropower. Austria and Sweden also use a lot of hydropower. On the **Danube** between **Serbia** and **Romania** lie the **Iron Gates**. There the river cuts through the Carpathians, and two large power plants dam it.

Hydropower plants produce electricity without giving off much **CO₂**. They often last for many decades. But dams change **valleys and rivers**. It becomes harder for fish to migrate upstream. That is why **fish ladders** are built today and care is taken to make sure enough water stays in the riverbed.

gewusst: At 285 metres, the Grande Dixence is almost as tall as the Eiffel Tower in Paris.
Hundreds of years ago people were already using water wheels to drive mills and saws.

teile.einleitung: Cyprus is an island in the far east of the Mediterranean. It is the third-largest island in the Mediterranean and has been a member of the European Union since 2004. Since 1974 the island has been divided into a northern and a southern part.
wichtigste: Cyprus is the third-largest island in the Mediterranean.
The capital is Nicosia in the middle of the island.
Since 2008 people in the Republic of Cyprus have paid in euros.
Most people speak Greek, and the second official language is Turkish.
Since 1974 the island has been divided.
Halloumi is a cheese from Cyprus.
The metal copper is named after the island.

abschnitte.text: Cyprus covers around **9,250 square kilometres**, so a little under a quarter of the size of Switzerland. Only **Sicily** and **Sardinia** are larger in the Mediterranean. The island lies in the far east of the Mediterranean. To the north, the coast of **Turkey** is only about 70 kilometres away. The capital is **Nicosia** in the middle of the island. There are beaches, but also mountains such as the **Troodos Mountains**.

According to Greek legend, the goddess **Aphrodite** rose from the sea foam on the coast of Cyprus. In ancient times a lot of **copper** was mined on Cyprus. The Latin name “cuprum” for copper comes from the name of the island. Over the course of history many powers ruled over Cyprus, most recently Great Britain. In **1960** Cyprus became **independent**.

In **1974** **Turkey** occupied the north of the island after a **coup**. Since then Cyprus has been divided. A **buffer zone** monitored by the **UN** separates the two parts, and it even runs through the middle of Nicosia. In the south live mainly Greek-speaking people, in the north mainly Turkish-speaking people. To this day there are negotiations about reunification.

Cyprus became a member of the **European Union** in **2004**, together with nine other countries. EU law, however, applies only in the south, which is controlled by the government. Since **2008** people there have paid in **euros**. Most people speak **Greek**, and the second official language is **Turkish**. Many tourists, including from Switzerland, spend their holidays there.

A well-known food from Cyprus is the cheese **halloumi**. It is firm and slightly salty. When **grilled** it does not melt but turns golden brown on the outside. That is why people like to put it straight onto the grill or into the pan. You can also buy it in Swiss shops.

gewusst: The word “copper” comes from the name of the island of Cyprus.
Nicosia is a capital city through which a border zone monitored by the UN runs.

teile.einleitung: Albedo tells you how strongly a surface reflects sunlight. Light surfaces such as snow and ice throw back a lot of light, while dark surfaces such as water or forest take in a lot of it. Albedo plays an important part in the Earth’s climate.
wichtigste: Albedo measures how much light a surface reflects.
Light surfaces such as snow and ice have a high albedo.
Dark surfaces such as the sea have a low albedo.
When sea ice melts, the dark water takes in more heat.
This makes even more ice melt, which strengthens the warming.

abschnitte.text: The word **albedo** comes from the Latin “albus”, meaning white. It describes what share of the sunlight a surface **reflects**. Fresh **snow** reflects most of the light and has a high albedo. The **sea** or a dark **forest**, on the other hand, swallow a lot of light and have a low albedo. You know this from summer: a black T-shirt gets warmer in the sun than a white one.

In the **Arctic** a lot of **sea ice** floats. It reflects a large part of the sunlight. When it melts, the **dark seawater** comes to light. This takes in much more solar energy and warms up. As a result even more ice melts.

In this way a cycle arises that reinforces itself. Experts call it a **feedback**, here the **ice-albedo feedback**. It is one reason why the Arctic is warming faster than most other regions of the Earth. Something similar applies in the Alps: when snow and glaciers disappear, the darker ground is heated up more strongly.

gewusst: Fresh snow often reflects more than 80 per cent of the sunlight, while open sea reflects only a small part of it.

teile.einleitung: Spitsbergen is the largest island of the Svalbard archipelago far in the north, in the Arctic Ocean. Svalbard belongs to Norway, but a special treaty also allows other states to carry out economic activity there. A large part of the land is covered by glaciers, and polar bears live there.
wichtigste: Spitsbergen is the largest island of the Svalbard archipelago.
The main town is Longyearbyen.
Willem Barentsz sighted the island in 1596 and gave it its name.
The Svalbard Treaty of 1920 allows all the states that signed it to mine under equal conditions.
About 60 per cent of the land area is covered by glaciers.
Outside the settlements, people protect themselves from polar bears with rifles.

abschnitte.text: **Svalbard** is a group of islands in the Arctic Ocean, halfway between Norway and the North Pole. In the narrower sense, the name **Spitsbergen** refers to the largest island of this archipelago. About **60 per cent** of the land area is covered by **glaciers**. In winter it stays dark for months, and in summer the midnight sun shines.

The Dutch seafarer **Willem Barentsz** sighted the islands in **1596**. He called them Spitsbergen, meaning “pointed mountains”, because of the sharp peaks. The **Svalbard Treaty** of **1920** laid down that the islands belong to Norway. At the same time, all the states that signed the treaty may be **economically active** there under equal conditions, for example by mining. Switzerland has also signed the treaty.

The main town is **Longyearbyen**. There is a school, an airport and a university there. The settlement of **Barentsburg** is run by a Russian mining company, and coal was mined there for a long time. **Ny-Ålesund** in the north-west is today mainly an international **research station**. Scientists from many countries study climate, ice and the atmosphere there.

In a mountain near Longyearbyen lies the **Svalbard Global Seed Vault**. This is a vault for **seeds** from all over the world. Seeds of grain, vegetables and many other crops are stored there. The cold inside the mountain helps to keep them for a long time. If a plant variety is lost somewhere, it can be grown again from these seeds.

**Polar bears** live on Spitsbergen. They can be dangerous to people. That is why people outside the settlements usually carry a **rifle** for protection or are accompanied by armed guides. The polar bears themselves are protected. The rifle is only for emergencies.

gewusst: Longyearbyen is one of the northernmost towns in the world.
Seeds from almost every country on Earth are stored in the Spitsbergen seed vault.

teile.einleitung: Stockholm is the capital of Sweden. The city is built on many islands, where Lake Mälaren flows into the Baltic Sea. Because of the many waterways, it is sometimes called the “Venice of the North”.
wichtigste: Stockholm is the capital of Sweden.
The city is built on many islands and lies on the Baltic Sea.
The old town is called Gamla Stan.
An old warship stands in the Vasa Museum.
Nobel Prizes are presented in Stockholm every year.
The metro is known for art in many stations.

abschnitte.text: Stockholm is built on **many islands**. The city lies where the large lake **Mälaren** meets the **Baltic Sea**. Many bridges connect the districts. Because of the many waterways, Stockholm is sometimes called the **“Venice of the North”**. Off the city lies the Stockholm archipelago with thousands of small islands.

The old town is called **Gamla Stan**, which means “Old Town”. It lies on an island in the centre. There are narrow lanes, colourful houses and small squares. At the edge of the old town stands the large **Royal Palace**. There you can see the guard, which is regularly changed.

In the **Vasa Museum** stands a real, old **warship**. The Vasa sank in **1628** on her very first voyage, shortly after leaving the harbour. For more than 300 years she lay on the sea floor. In 1961 she was raised. Because the water of the Baltic contains little salt, the wood has been well preserved.

Every year on 10 December the **Nobel Prizes** are presented in Stockholm, except for the Nobel Peace Prize, which is awarded in Oslo. For children there is the **Junibacken** museum. There you can experience the world of **Pippi Longstocking** and other characters by Astrid Lindgren. You even ride through her stories on a little train.

The **metro** of Stockholm is called the Tunnelbana. It is known for **art in many stations**. Some stations look like painted caves in rock, with bright colours on walls and ceilings. The metro is therefore often called the longest art gallery in the world.

gewusst: The ship Vasa sank after sailing only about 1,300 metres.
In the middle of Stockholm you can swim in the water at many places in summer.

teile.einleitung: A Sámi Parliament (Sameting) is an elected parliament of the Sami. Such representative bodies exist in Norway, Sweden and Finland. They stand up for the language, culture and rights of the Sami.
wichtigste: The elected representative bodies of the Sami are called Sameting.
There is a Sameting in Norway, in Sweden and in Finland.
The Norwegian Sameting sits in Karasjok.
Sami who enter themselves in an electoral register may vote.
The Sameting members look after language, culture and reindeer herding.

abschnitte.text: A **Sameting** is an **elected representative body** of the Sami. Sami who have themselves entered in a separate **electoral register** may vote. The Samediggi are not state parliaments but represent the concerns of the Sami towards the government. As in a parliament, there are parties and lists. Elections are held every four years.

The **Norwegian Sameting** was founded in **1989** and has its seat in **Karasjok**. Its building is modelled on the shape of a Sami tent. In **Sweden** there has been a Sameting since 1993, with its seat in Kiruna. In **Finland** there has been a Sameting since 1996, and its cultural centre is in Inari. In Russia there is no such officially recognised body.

The Sameting members promote the **Sami languages**, for example in schools and the media. They support culture, art and traditions. They give their opinion when the state plans laws that affect the Sami, for example on **reindeer herding** or the use of land. The three Samediggi also work together across borders.

gewusst: The building of the Norwegian Sameting in Karasjok is modelled on a Sami tent.
